They carry 45 long tons (46 tonnes) of diesel fuel, enabling a range of 5,000 nautical miles at 10 knots when operating at snorkel depth.

The Abtao-class submarine comprised four boats: Abtao, Dos de Mayo, and two others. The class was armed with six 21-inch (533 mm) torpedo tubes, four in the bow and two aft. Abtao and Dos de Mayo were equipped with a 5-inch (127 mm)/25-caliber deck gun mounted abaft the sail, and the gun was manually sighted. All four boats carried the SS-2A radar as well as BQR-3 and BQA-1A sonar systems. In 1981, the batteries were replaced, and subsequently the Thomson Sintra Eledone active/passive intercept sonar was installed. The crew complement consisted of 40 officers and ratings.

Human monocytotropic ehrlichiosis commonly presents with fever, headache, malaise, and myalgia. Compared with human granulocytic anaplasmosis, the rash occurs more frequently in HME. Laboratory evaluation often reveals thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, and elevated liver tests.

Management of suspected human monocytotropic ehrlichiosis emphasizes not delaying treatment while awaiting definitive laboratory confirmation, since early initiation of doxycycline is associated with improved outcomes. Doxycycline remains the treatment of choice for this infection.

John Walsh, an 18th-century associate of the English East India Company, joined the company at the age of fifteen and soon became the private secretary to Robert Clive, maintaining a close advisory role during his campaigns in Bengal. In the 1757 Plassey campaign against Siraj ud-Daulah, Walsh was awarded prize money totaling £56,000, and when he returned to England in 1759 he did so with a substantial fortune, estimated at about £147,000, using his wealth to pursue aristocratic influence through land ownership and political connections. In late 1764 he purchased the Warfield Park estate near Bracknell, Berkshire, and spent two years refurbishing the property. Walsh also served as the Member of Parliament for Worcester from 1761 to 1780, continuing to support Clive and attempting to establish a parliamentary interest favorable to him.

John Walsh developed scientific interests in his later life, with a particular focus on electric fishes. He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1770, and in 1773 was awarded the Royal Society's Copley Medal for a paper on the electrical properties of torpedo fish.

In the United Kingdom in 2006, a poverty-line concept based on low pay defined earners at or below 60% of the full-time median earnings, which corresponded to about £6.67 per hour. At this rate, a 35-hour working week would amount to just over £12,000 per year, before tax or National Insurance. However, figures from April 2006 indicate that a 35-hour week would have earned roughly £9,191 annually before tax and NI. Among employed people, more than five million individuals—about 23% of all workers—were paid less than £6.67 per hour, highlighting the scale of low pay relative to the proposed threshold.

The poverty line denotes a threshold of income or consumption used to identify individuals in poverty. In developed countries, some people living near this line may reside in poor conditions or substandard housing situated in urban areas with elevated crime. Their monthly finances are strained by insufficient wages, high debt burdens, or unemployment, making it difficult to cover essential bills and necessities. Even so, they are beneficiaries of the country's broad infrastructure and public services, yet their overall lifestyle remains below the national median. When compared to more affluent compatriots within the same country, or to wealthy individuals in less developed nations with lower living costs, their standard of living illustrates the sensitivity of poverty assessments to both price levels and social protections.

ATP Tour 500 constitutes the fourth-highest level of annual men's professional tennis tournaments on the ATP Tour, ranking behind the Grand Slam events, the ATP Finals, and the ATP Masters 1000 series. Tournaments in this tier award 500 ranking points to the singles champion, which explains the designation. The tier has undergone several name changes over time, having been called the ATP World Tour 500, the ATP International Series Gold, and the ATP Championship Series.

As of 2025, the ATP Tour 500 series comprises sixteen tournaments. The singles main draw is typically 32 players, although the Washington Open features a 48-player field; the doubles main draw is set at 16 teams. The circuit imposes participation requirements on leading players, who must enter at least four 500-level events, including at least one held after the US Open. Failure to meet the minimum or to participate in a post‑US Open 500 event results in zero ranking points toward the player's world ranking for each missing event.

The 1904 South Carolina gubernatorial election, held on November 8, 1904, was the contest to elect the state’s governor. The nomination went to Duncan Clinch Heyward, who faced no opposition in the Democratic primary, nor in the general election. As a result, Heyward won a second two-year term as governor.

The general election in South Carolina was held on November 8, 1904. Incumbent governor Duncan Clinch Heyward was reelected to a second term, with the contest running unopposed. Voter turnout rose compared with the previous gubernatorial election, a gain attributed to the concurrent presidential election appearing on the ballot that year.

The sixth Bamum script, known as A Ka U Ku after its first four glyphs, was developed circa 1910. It comprises 82 characters and ten digits, signaling a transition to a full syllabic writing system capable of distinguishing roughly 160 syllables. This shift enabled a more comprehensive representation of the language and was used to record vital events and legal matters, including births, marriages, deaths, and court rulings.

Rii Nyi Mfw' Men, the fifth system of the Bamum script, was developed circa 1907–1908. It comprises 195 characters and a set of ten digits. The script was employed in a Bible translation. The initial five Bamum scripts are closely related, having evolved from a sequence of progressively simplified pictographic proto-writing with logographic elements.

The South Africa national soccer team represented South Africa as hosts of the 2010 FIFA World Cup, competing in Group A with Mexico, Uruguay, and France, the runners-up of the 2006 edition. In their opening match, they drew 1–1 with Mexico after a long-range strike by Siphiwe Tshabalala put them ahead. The team then suffered a 3–0 defeat to Uruguay in their second group game. Mexico’s later victory over France influenced South Africa’s chances of advancing, and the host nation achieved a win against France in the final group match. Ultimately, South Africa were eliminated at the group-stage phase, becoming the first host nation to fail to progress beyond the first round.

South Africa, as host nation of the 2010 FIFA World Cup, recorded a 2–1 victory over France, a 1–1 draw with Mexico, and a 0–3 defeat to Uruguay in the group stage. These results left the team without advancement to the Round of 16, making South Africa the first host nation to fail to progress beyond the group phase of a World Cup.

Saint Petersburg provides a regular rapid-bus link between Pulkovo Airport and the Moskovskaya metro station, facilitating direct access from the airport to the city’s rapid transit network. The routes serving this corridor are 39, 39E, and K39, offering frequent service for travelers arriving at Pulkovo. In addition, a taxi service operates on a 24/7 basis, supplying round-the-clock transportation options within the city.

Saint Petersburg emerged from Peter the Great’s initiative to secure a seaport for trade with Europe. He regarded Arkhangelsk as insufficient for Russia’s needs; as the nation’s principal port, Arkhangelsk lay on the White Sea in the far north and was shut to shipping during the winter months. In response, Peter pursued the establishment of a Baltic port that would provide a year‑round outlet for maritime commerce with Europe.

On 10 March 1526, Francisco Pizarro departed Panama with two ships, about 160 men, and several horses, reaching as far as the San Juan River in Colombia. The expedition then split, with Pizarro remaining to explore the newly encountered territory while Gonzalo de Almagro returned to Panama to secure reinforcements. Pizarro’s Piloto Mayor, Bartolomé Ruiz, continued the voyage southward, and after crossing the equator he seized a balsa raft carrying natives from Tumbes. The raft bore textiles, ceramics, and quantities of gold, silver, and emeralds, making Ruiz’s findings central to the aims of the second expedition. Some of the raft’s inhabitants were taken aboard Ruiz’s ship to serve as interpreters.

During the initial phase, Diego de Almagro set out to recruit men, secure supplies, and would later join Pizarro’s venture. Governor Pedro Arias Dávila of Panama gave approval in principle for the exploration of South America. Pizarro’s first expedition ended in failure as the party sailed along the Pacific coast and reached only as far as present-day Colombia. The difficulties stemmed from adverse weather, shortages of food, and clashes with hostile indigenous groups, with Almagro even losing an eye to an arrow. The route yielded toponyms that reflected their hardships, including Puerto Deseado (the desired port), Puerto del Hambre (port of hunger), and Punta Quemado/Puebla Quemado (burned port). These names underscored the challenges faced, and fear of further hostile encounters such as the Battle of Punta Quemada led Pizarro to discontinue the first voyage and return to Panama.

Within the laryngeal musculature, the lower and deeper fibers differentiate to form a triangular band that inserts into the vocal process of the arytenoid cartilage and the adjacent portion of its anterior surface. This band is referred to as the vocalis. It lies parallel to the vocal ligament and remains adherent to it.

The ventricularis muscle is composed of only a few fibers that extend along the wall of the laryngeal ventricle, originating from the lateral wall of the arytenoid cartilage and inserting on the side of the epiglottis.

In 1758, Washington participated in the Forbes Expedition aimed at capturing Fort Duquesne. During the campaign, a friendly-fire incident occurred when his unit was mistaken for French by another British force, resulting in 14 dead and 26 wounded. Despite this mishap, the French abandoned Fort Duquesne, and the British achieved a major strategic victory by gaining control of the Ohio Valley. Washington resigned his commission upon returning to Virginia in December 1758, and he did not resume military service until the outbreak of the American Revolution in 1775.

George Washington commanded Continental forces during the siege of Boston and proved pivotal in securing the British withdrawal by deploying Henry Knox’s artillery to Dorchester Heights, a position that commanded a view of the city and compelled the Crown forces to evacuate. He prepared in detail to assault Boston from Cambridge if the British should attempt to retake the position, maintaining an attack plan tailored to possible contingencies. After the British evacuated by sea, Washington remained uncertain of their true destination, Halifax, Nova Scotia among the possibilities. Believing the fleet to be aimed at New York City, Howe’s eventual destination, Washington redirected much of the army northward to counter that move.

Nemeton denotes a sacred site in Gaulish and Celtic contexts, with a well-known instance located in the Névet forest near Locronan in Brittany. The term has cognates in Modern Breton as neved, meaning 'sanctuary,' and in Welsh as nyfed, reflecting its shared Celtic heritage. Archaeological remains identified as nemeta have also been reported at Gournay-sur-Aronde in the Oise, illustrating its geographic spread within ancient Gaul. The label survives in several French place-names, such as Novionemetum, formed from noviios meaning 'new,' which subsequently evolved to Nonant and Nonant-le-Pin; compounds like Nemeto-pons yield Nampont; and Nemetodurum, interpreted as 'door' or 'forum of the temple,' gives Nanterre. In Paris, Namet has been proposed by some scholars as an ancient name for the Quartier du Temple on the Right Bank, a claim rooted in a doggerel from 1270.

A nemeton, plural nemeta, denotes a sacred space in ancient Celtic religion. These spaces were predominantly situated in natural settings, often in sacred groves, and the term likewise referred to a wider range of ritual sites such as shrines and temples. Evidence for nemeta rests chiefly on inscriptions and toponymy (place-names). Toponymic attestations linked to nemeton occur across the Celtic world, from Galicia in the Iberian Peninsula to Scotland, and as far as central Turkey. The term is etymologically related to the Nemetes, a Rhine-area tribe, and their goddess Nemetona.

Águas Belas, a name meaning “Beautiful Waters” in Portuguese, originated from a judge’s commentary delivered during a visit to the city, in which he expressed admiration for the exceptional quality of the local water.

Águas Belas has a diversified economy driven by industry, commerce, and agribusiness. Within the agribusiness sector, cultivation concentrates on beans, corn, and manioc, forming a central agricultural activity for the area. In addition, livestock farming is extensive, with cattle, goats, and sheep raised alongside horses, pigs, and poultry, including chickens.

The watt is the SI unit of power, named in honour of the Scottish inventor James Watt. The proposal to designate the unit originated with C. William Siemens in August 1882, delivered in his President's Address to the Fifty-Second Congress of the British Association for the Advancement of Science. Siemens noted that practical units are historically named after prominent physicists and proposed watt as the unit of power. He defined the watt as the power conveyed when a current of one ampere passes through a potential difference of one volt, thereby formalizing the relation P = IV.

Picowatts are used primarily in fields involving extremely low power levels, including radio and radar receivers, acoustics, and radio astronomy. In acoustics, a picowatt is the internationally accepted reference quantity for sound power when expressed in decibels, acting as the reference power against which sound power levels are measured on the decibel scale.

In Australia and New Zealand, government auctions of the 3G radio spectrum were conducted, but the bidding results were unusually modest, prompting strong suspicions of collusion among the operator groups. The alleged collusive behavior reportedly encompassed coordinated low bids and the secret development of network-sharing agreements between competing carriers.

Five years after the 1996 Telecommunications Act, the industry embarked on an extensive expansion funded largely by debt, with telecom companies investing more than $500 billion to extend fiber optic networks, upgrade switching infrastructure, and deploy wireless systems. Government involvement in regions such as the Dulles Technology Corridor included targeted funding and regulatory advantages intended to accelerate build-out. Nevertheless, the pace of capacity expansion far outpaced demand growth, creating an oversupply scenario. In 2000, 3G spectrum auctions yielded substantial sums: the United Kingdom’s April sale raised about £22.5 billion, and Germany’s August sale raised around £30 billion, while the United States experienced difficulties in the 1999 auction, which had to be re-run after bidder defaults and ultimately produced proceeds only about 10 percent of the original prices. As the dot-com bubble burst, financing tightened and many operators faced bankruptcies or restructurings due to high leverage. Overall, industry debt and losses totaled roughly $1 trillion, much of which was unlikely to be repaid, a point noted by FCC Chairman Powell in testimony on July 30, 2002, with bond investors recovering just over 20 percent of their holdings.

New York City exhibits a transportation pattern dominated by public transit, with mass transit widely used by residents. In 2005, 54.6% of New Yorkers commuted to work by mass transit. By comparison, in the rest of the United States, about 91% of commuters travel by automobile. Among large U.S. cities, workers in the New York City metropolitan area spend an average of 6 hours and 18 minutes commuting per week, the longest figure. Fifty-two percent of New York City households do not own a car, and 22% of Manhattan residents own a car. The substantial reliance on transit is associated with lower transportation spending, with New York City saving approximately $19 billion annually relative to other urban Americans.

On September 11, 1776, a peaceful overture was proposed at the Conference House on Staten Island, where American delegates including Benjamin Franklin met with British General Lord Howe in an effort to negotiate a settlement. Soon after the British occupation of New York began, the Great Fire of New York broke out, destroying roughly 500 buildings—about a quarter of the city’s structures—and Trinity Church was among the losses.

In northwestern medieval India, Buddhist communities extended into the Himalayan regions and areas adjacent to Central Asia, where they interacted with and helped sustain regional trade networks. The scholar Lars Fogelin has highlighted this trade-support role as a characteristic of Buddhist establishments in these zones. With Islamic invasions and expansions, and as Central Asians adopted Islam, financial backing for Buddhist monasteries derived from trade routes waned. The resulting decline in revenue undermined Buddhism’s survival and growth in the region. The arrival of Islam also ended royal patronage to monastic Buddhism, while Muslims displaced Buddhists in long-distance commerce, eroding another major patronage source for Buddhist institutions.

During the history of Buddhism in India, royal courts patronized both Buddhist and Shaiva traditions, yielding a diverse body of Vajrayana literature. The Mañjusrimulakalpa, later classified within the Kriyatantra, asserts that mantras originating from Shaiva, Garuda, and Vaishnava tantras can be effective for Buddhists because they are said to have been taught by Manjushri. In the Guhyasiddhi of Padmavajra, associated with the Guhyasamaja, the text prescribes acting as a Shaiva guru and initiating adherents into Shaiva Siddhanta scriptures and mandalas. Samvara tantra texts adopted the pitha list from the Shaiva Tantrasadbhava, though a copying error occurred in which a deity was misidentified as a place. This convergence highlights the syncretic and intertextual dynamics of Indian Buddhist tantric literature within patronage networks.

Numerous experimental trials of the KLM scheme have been conducted, as documented in the literature. Although the protocol can in principle realize quantum operations with high success probabilities, achieving values very close to one necessitates a large number of sequential operations, which imposes substantial resource overhead. Consequently, the practical viability of the KLM protocol depends on the development of more efficient quantum gates that can perform the required functionality with fewer resources and greater reliability. The next section addresses this issue by focusing on the design and implementation of more efficient gates.

The Knill-Laflamme-Milburn (KLM) protocol is a scheme for linear-optics quantum computing that uses projective measurements with photodetectors to induce effective photon-photon interactions, enabling non-deterministic quantum gates. Central to the approach is a non-linear sign shift between two qubits implemented with two ancilla photons and post-selection. The probability of success for a single gate can be increased toward near-deterministic operation by employing entangled resource states prepared non-deterministically and performing quantum teleportation with single-qubit operations. If the single-gate success rate is too low, the required resources grow exponentially. The protocol utilizes quantum coding to reduce the encoding resources necessary to achieve a desired accuracy. This framework can render linear-optics quantum computing fault-tolerant against photon loss, detector inefficiency, and phase decoherence. When resource demands are kept modest, LOQC implemented via KLM is potentially scalable and competitive with other quantum computing platforms.

East Africa is one of the regions where Homo sapiens are believed to have lived early in human prehistory. In Kenya’s Olorgesailie site, evidence dating to approximately 320,000 years ago points to the early emergence of modern behaviors, including long-distance exchange networks involving obsidian, the use of pigments, and possible production of projectile points. Three studies published in 2018 on the site note that these behaviors are roughly contemporaneous with the appearance of the earliest Homo sapiens fossils in Africa, such as those from Jebel Irhoud and Florisbad. This concurrence has been interpreted as indicating that complex and modern behaviors may have originated in Africa around the time of Homo sapiens emergence.

East Africa is commonly regarded as a likely corridor for the Out of Africa migration, with the Bab-el-Mandeb strait identified as a possible gateway between Africa and the Arabian Peninsula. Today, the straits span about 12 miles (19 kilometers). Geological and paleoceanographic evidence indicates that roughly 50,000 years ago the channel was substantially narrower, while sea levels stood approximately 70 meters lower than present. Nevertheless, the straits were never fully closed, and there may have existed intermediate islands within the strait that could have been reached by simple rafts. These factors collectively inform hypotheses about early human dispersal from East Africa.

In a collegiate university, the head of a college, sometimes described as the head of house, serves as the senior administrator and chief figure responsible for the governance and overall management of the college. The exact title for this role varies among institutions, reflecting distinct traditions and organizational structures. Common designations include dean, master, president, principal, provost, rector, and warden, among others, with some colleges employing unique terms rooted in their history. Through this leadership, the head of the college oversees academic affairs, financial management, and strategic planning within the broader university framework.

Across Durham University, Lancaster University, and the University of Roehampton, the heads of colleges participate in their universities’ senate as ex officio members, a status granted by virtue of holding the office rather than through a separate election to the senate. Ex officio membership denotes an automatic association with the governing body resulting from incumbency of the post. The rule applies universally to all heads of colleges, with no exceptions. The article situates the President (college) role within the governance framework of these institutions.

Often referred to as the Ramadan Revolution, the 1963 Iraqi coup saw Ba’athist officers overthrow Prime Minister Abd al-Karim Qasim and reshape Iraqi politics. As of 2021, CIA operations in Iraq remain largely classified, and scholars are divided over the extent of American involvement in planning or supporting the coup. Some writers contend that the CIA assisted the Ba’th in overthrowing Qasim, but the bulk of evidence points to the CIA not being behind the February 1963 coup. Others maintain that declassified U.S. documents show no direct involvement, while proponents of a more expansive interpretation argue that the CIA’s role has long been treated as an open secret, and that declassified materials substantiate plausible American involvement. There is also a line of analysis citing substantial evidence of CIA contacts with Iraqi Ba’athists in the early 1960s and assistance in planning the uprising. Still others observe that Washington backed Ba’athist officers, though the complete degree of U.S. responsibility cannot be determined from the existing record; and while the United States did not initiate the 14 Ramadan coup, it may have condoned or contributed to the subsequent violence.

Often described as the Ramadan Revolution, the 1963 Iraqi coup d'etat was propelled by Ba'athist factions that drew on a university-based network, including a Ba'athist student group at the University of Baghdad whose activities helped trigger the February 8, 1963 strike. Declassified documents indicate that U.S. officials actively cultivated Ba'athist networks and regarded certain Iraqi figures as assets: Salih Mahdi Ammash, head of the Army Bureau, who maintained cordial relations with Western and embassy staff, and Hazim Jawad, involved in clandestine printing and propaganda, whom U.S. officials later described as favorable to American interests. Iraqi and Syrian Ba’athists depicted cooperation with the CIA and the United States to overthrow Qasim as comparable to a Lenin-style arrival facilitated by American assistance, a view echoed by Ali Salih al-Sa’di, who stated that the Iraqi Ba’ath came to power on a CIA train. Jamal al-Atassi conveyed to Malik Mufti that Syrian and Iraqi Ba’athists likewise framed their CIA/U.S. cooperation in that metaphor. James E. Akins, the U.S. ambassador to Saudi Arabia who had served in Baghdad from 1961 to 1964, testified to Ba’ath–CIA contacts and to the revolution receiving U.S. support in the form of money and equipment, with financial assistance being the predominant and not openly acknowledged component. A CIA officer named Gibson involved in planning a coup against Qasim later denied direct involvement in the Ba’athists’ actions, arguing that CIA efforts remained in the planning stage. Taken together, the period from 1961 to 1964 highlights a close, often covert, U.S. engagement with Iraqi Ba’athists surrounding the 1963 coup.

Beja sits on the site of the Roman towns Pax Julia (Paca) and is surrounded by remnants of ancient Roman walls, portions of which have been restored. The Roman Catholic Diocese of Beja was established on 10 June 1770. In 1162, Beja was wrested from Islamic rulers by Afonso I of Portugal. Beja Cathedral is an historic church that has undergone extensive modernization, with the original date of its founding uncertain.

The Roman Catholic Diocese of Beja, located in Beja, has a historical tradition linking its early episcopal succession to Isidorus Pacensis, an eighth-century chronicler. Traditional accounts hold that he served as bishop of Beja, but this attribution is now contested by scholars, who question the reliability of the sources and the precise identification of his episcopal see.

Lisa Vogel, founder and longtime organizer of the Michigan Womyn's Music Festival, defended the festival's week-long space for individuals who were born female and continue to live as women, describing it as a healthy, whole, and loving environment for those with that experience. She argued that labeling the space as transphobic was misplaced, drawing analogies to claims that a women-of-color tent is racist or that a transgender-only space is misogynistic. Vogel also endorsed the politics and culture of maintaining separate time and space for this community. In 2006, she stated that there is nothing transphobic about spending a week with women who were born as women and have lived their lives as women.

In a fall 1994 issue of The Village Voice, Gretchen Phillips, a musician and Festival kitchen worker who co-founded the band Two Nice Girls, discusses her impressions of the Michigan Womyn's Music Festival. She notes the event's notable display of nudity, observing exposed breasts and bare buttocks among attendees. Phillips entered the weekend with the aim of using the experience to examine her own body image issues. She describes Michigan as a crucial source of energy for the year ahead and structures her schedule to be there each August. The experience yielded lessons that were both enjoyable and challenging, informing her perspective in multiple ways.

Sigh No More is the debut studio album by Mumford & Sons, which achieved substantial commercial success in both the United Kingdom and the United States, selling more than one million copies in the UK and more than three million copies in the United States. In the United States, sales were 626,000 copies in 2010 and 1,282,000 copies in 2011, with total U.S. sales exceeding 3.2 million by May 2015. The album also became the second debut album to sell one million digital copies, after Lady Gaga's The Fame, with digital sales of about 1.66 million.

Sigh No More is the debut studio album by the British folk rock band Mumford & Sons. It was released in the United Kingdom on 2 October 2009 and in the United States and Canada on 16 February 2010. On the UK Albums Chart, the record entered at number 11 and eventually rose to a peak of number 2 on 20 February 2011 in its 72nd week, following the band's Brit Awards Album of the Year win. In the United States, the album peaked at number 2 on the Billboard 200 in early 2011.
Neilson Powless, a professional cyclist born at Eglin Air Force Base, is the first rider of Native American ancestry to compete in the Tour de France.

Eglin AFB Auxiliary Field No. 6, also known as Biancur Field, is the site that hosts Camp James E. Rudder. The installation serves as the home of the United States Army's 6th Ranger Training Battalion (6th RTB). The 6th RTB conducts the final phase of the U.S. Army Ranger Course. The Ranger Course lasts 61 days and is divided into three phases, each of which takes place at different geographical and environmental locations.

Abai is a Murutic language spoken on the island of Borneo by the Abai people in the villages of Sembuak and Tubu. Although it belongs to the Murutic language group, Ethnologue classifies it as a Putoh dialect, a misclassification that has been noted in linguistic references.

Rihanna showed an early interest in the arts and later signed with Def Jam Recordings. Her debut albums Music of the Sun (2005) and A Girl Like Me (2006) both reached the top ten of the US Billboard 200, yielding the singles "Pon de Replay" (peaking at number two on the US Billboard Hot 100) and "SOS" (reaching number one). She subsequently adopted a more mature image and shifted toward dance-pop and R&B with Good Girl Gone Bad (2007) and its Reloaded reissue (2008). From Good Girl Gone Bad, several US Hot 100 number-one singles emerged, including "Umbrella," "Take a Bow," and "Disturbia."

In early 2012, Rihanna contributed guest vocals to Coldplay's "Princess of China" and Drake's "Take Care." In February 2012, she and Kanye West won the Grammy Award for Best Rap/Sung Collaboration for "All of the Lights," and the same month she was named Best International Female Solo Artist at the Brit Awards for the second consecutive year. In March 2012, she released two remixes with Chris Brown—"Birthday Cake" and the remix of "Turn Up the Music"—amid criticism stemming from their history of domestic violence. In September 2012, the music video for "We Found Love" won MTV's Video of the Year, making Rihanna the first woman to receive the honor more than once. In 2013, the same video won the Grammy Award for Best Short Form Music Video.

RNIB Connect Radio operates with its main studios in Scotland, while additional studios are located in Grimaldi House, London. The service transmits programming across the United Kingdom and worldwide, and maintains a notable listenership in the United States and Canada.

RNIB Connect Radio is an online radio service operated by the Royal National Institute of Blind People (RNIB). It was launched in November 2003 under the name VIP on Air, initially broadcasting two hours per day; the schedule was later extended to four hours daily. In 2007 the service underwent a revamp, was renamed, and relaunched as Insight Radio.

Ōnami was a Japanese destroyer of the Yūgumo class. Its principal armament consisted of six Type 3 127 mm guns arranged in three twin turrets, with a pair of superfiring mounts aft and the remaining turret positioned forward of the superstructure. Although the guns could elevate to 75 degrees to engage aircraft, the class overall suffered from weak anti-aircraft performance due to a slow rate of fire, slow gun traverse, and the absence of a high-angle fire-control system. The initial anti-aircraft setup comprised four Type 96 25 mm guns in two twin mounts, with additional AA mounts added later in the war. For torpedo offensive capability, Ōnami carried eight 610 mm torpedo tubes in two quadruple traversing mounts, with one reload provided for each tube. In terms of anti-submarine warfare, the destroyer was equipped with two depth charge throwers and carried a total of 36 depth charges.
Ōnami (大波) was a Yūgumo-class destroyer in the Imperial Japanese Navy that served during World War II. The name translates to "billow wave," reflecting the idea of large, rough seas.

The Roman letter B derives from the Greek capital Beta, reaching the Italic world through successive Etruscan and Cumaean variants. Beta itself was a Greek adaptation of the Phoenician letter bēt, whose name signifies “house.” The Phoenician bēt arose as a modified form of a Proto-Sinaitic glyph that was inspired by the hieroglyph associated with the concept of a house; in Egyptian practice, the hieroglyph for the consonant /b/ is depicted as a foot and a calf. The Hebrew letter bet, by contrast, is considered a separate development from the Phoenician letter rather than a direct continuation.

B is a letter of the Latin alphabet whose historical phonology reflects Grimm's Law, a principle describing the regular shifts of certain Proto-Indo-European consonants in Germanic languages. Consequently, cognates in other Indo-European languages may appear with reflexes such as bh, p, f, or φ, depending on the lineage and language. The word for “brother” is a common illustration of these variations: English shows the initial b, while Latin renders it as frater and Greek as phrater (φρ), with other branches preserving bh- forms. In modern English usage, the letter B is relatively uncommon, accounting for about 1.5% of words and ranking as the seventh least frequent letter, behind V, K, J, X, Q, and Z.

Juan de Lángara was a Spanish admiral who headed the Spanish Navy. During the era of exploration, Spanish explorers charted portions of the coast of what is now British Columbia, Canada, and named land formations after him. His name persists in British Columbia toponyms, including Langara Island off the province’s northern coast. In Canada, Langara College in Vancouver carries the Langara designation; it was founded in 1970 as the Langara campus of Vancouver Community College and later became an independent public college in 1994.

Juan de Lángara was a Spanish admiral who played a pivotal role during the Toulon evacuation of 1793, when British and Spanish forces under Sir Sidney Smith sought to destroy the arsenal and harbor ships as they were withdrawn. He commanded the rear-guard, directing actions in which the arsenal was blown up and several warships were refloated and subsequently sent to Britain. In the same operation, Admiral Samuel Hood managed to ensure the escape of fifteen French ships from Toulon before the city fell. Later, on 14 February 1795, after a six-hour pursuit aboard the Reina Luisa, Lángara captured the 32-gun French frigate Helène.
On 31 January 1992, the RSFSR Football Federation, described at the time as supposedly still existing and led by president Yuri Nyrkov, announced that a conference would be held on 8 February 1992.

The Russian Football Union (RFU) is governed by a board of directors that is led by chairman Nikita Simonyan, and the board also includes the director general, Aleksandr Alayev. The RFU is a member of FIFA and UEFA, and it maintains a relationship with the International Olympic Committee (IOC).

Root locus analysis is a graphical method in control theory and stability theory used to examine how the roots of the characteristic equation of a linear time-invariant system move as a system parameter varies, typically the feedback gain. It is employed as a stability criterion in classical control theory by showing how the closed-loop poles shift in the complex s-plane, thereby indicating regions of stability. The technique was developed by Walter R. Evans. In practice, the root locus plots the trajectories of the closed-loop transfer function poles in the complex plane as the gain parameter is varied, offering insights that are closely related to traditional pole–zero plots.

Root locus analysis examines the motion of closed-loop poles by solving for the variable z as the loop gain changes, thereby identifying how pole locations vary with gain. Real roots on the real axis correspond to breakaway or break-in points, indicating where poles detach from or return to the real axis as the gain is adjusted. When a solution yields complex poles, it indicates that no breakaway or reentry points on the real axis occur at that gain value. Breakaway points arise when two real poles coalesce on the real axis and subsequently move into the complex plane as the gain changes, while break-in points describe the opposite process, with poles moving from the complex plane back onto the real axis.

The Roman Rite, known in Latin as Ritus Rōmānus, is the principal liturgical tradition used for the ecclesiastical services of the Latin Church, which constitutes the largest sui iuris particular church within the Catholic Church. It governs the principal rites performed in liturgical celebrations, including the Roman Mass and the Liturgy of the Hours, and it also prescribes the manner in which sacraments and blessings are administered.

The Roman Rite maintains a fixed, doctrinally defined structure that governs liturgical celebration within the Latin Church. Within this framework, the Scripture readings are not static but shift daily in line with the liturgical calendar, ensuring selections reflect the season, feast, or saint commemorated. Antiphons for the entrance procession and for Communion also vary from day to day, mirroring the calendar’s particular observances. In addition, several other prayers are adjusted daily in accordance with the liturgical calendar. Together, these elements combine a stable framework with regular daily variation to support both continuity and the seasonal emphasis of the rite.

IEC 61355 defines a document kind classification code (DCC), a structured letter-based coding scheme that serves to classify documents of any kind. The system provides a uniform approach to indexing and retrieving documents across diverse fields, enabling consistent organization and reference.

IEC 61355-1, the part of the IEC 61355 standard titled Classification and designation of documents for plants, systems and equipment, establishes a framework for the uniform classification and designation of technical documents related to plants, systems and equipment. It provides rules and guidelines intended to ensure consistency in how documents are categorized and identified, with the classification and designation decisions based on the characteristic content of the information contained in the documents.

The Emancipation Statue, a sculpture by Karl Broodhagen, was unveiled in 1985 in Haggatt Hall, in the parish of St Michael, Barbados. The unveiling occurred 169 years after Bussa's rebellion of 1816. Although the monument is officially associated with emancipation, many Barbadians attribute it to Bussa and have nicknamed it "Bussa's Statue."

Bussa's rebellion arose during a period when Parliament was considering measures aimed at improving conditions for Caribbean slaves. Preparation for the uprising began after the House of Assembly discussed and rejected the Imperial Registry Bill in November 1815, a proposal that would have registered West Indian slaves. Historians believe that enslaved people viewed some parliamentary measures as potential steps toward emancipation, but the rebellions occurred in the absence of emancipation.

Blairgowrie and Rattray serves as the starting and finishing point of the Cateran Trail, a marked long-distance circular walk spanning 64 miles (103 kilometres). The route winds through Glenericht and Strathardle to Bridge of Cally, continues via Kirkmichael and Enochdhu, ascends over Ben Earb to Spittal of Glenshee, traverses Glenshee and Glenisla to Kirkton of Glenisla and Alyth, and returns to Blairgowrie. The trail is divided into five stages and can be completed in five days or less. In the annual Cateran Yomp, winners regularly complete the circuit in under eleven hours.

Newton Castle, situated on the western edge of Blairgowrie, serves as the residence of the chieftain of Clan Macpherson. Ardblair Castle, also located on Blairgowrie's western outskirts, is the home of the Blair Oliphant family.

In the early phase of the conflict, American forces advanced north from Manila and captured Caloocan on February 10. With Malolos under threat, the seat of the Philippine Republic was relocated to San Isidro in Nueva Ecija on March 29, but Malolos fell to American troops on March 31, leaving the city gutted by fires set by retreating forces. Aguinaldo and the core revolutionary government subsequently moved to San Isidro, while peace negotiations with the Schurman Commission failed amid a brief ceasefire in April–May 1899. On May 16, San Isidro likewise came under American control, prompting the core government to shift first to Bamban in Tarlac province and later to the town of Tarlac, before Aguinaldo’s party departed from Tarlac prior to its occupation later that year. Concurrently, American forces captured Calumpit, Bulacan on April 27, Apalit, Pampanga on May 4, and San Fernando, Pampanga on May 5, changes that contributed to the republic’s recurring relocation of its seat of government in response to military developments.
After Nueva Ecija was captured by American forces in 1899, the Casa Real de Tarlac served as the headquarters of the revolutionary capital.

Historically, South Africa's higher education system displayed a distinct split between universities and technikons (polytechnics), with separate trajectories for academic and technical education. Compounding this structure was a coexistence of institutions that primarily served particular racial and language communities, creating a segmented landscape along both disciplinary and demographic lines.

Within the Institute of Technology, the Nuclear Science Department of the Escuela Politécnica Nacional (EPN) stands as Ecuador's sole academic unit devoted to nuclear science. It is supported by substantial infrastructure and houses irradiation facilities, including a cobalt-60 source and capabilities for electron beam processing, which enable both research and practical applications in radiation technologies.

Garius, sometimes referred to as Garios, was a town in ancient Paphlagonia. Its Greek name was Γάριος. The site stood 80 stadia east of Callistratia and was inhabited during the Roman and Byzantine periods.

On October 18, 1867, the USS Ossipee arrived at Sitka with the Russian Commissioner Captain Alexis Pestchouroff and the American Commissioner General Lovell Rousseau aboard. The ceremony was attended by roughly 250 American soldiers, 80 Russian soldiers, the Russian-American Company’s Chief Manager Prince Maksutov and his wife, and local residents. It was held at the flagstaff in front of the governor's residence on Baranof Castle Hill (Baronov). During the event, the Russian flag was lowered and the United States flag was raised.

Department of Alaska refers to the administrative framework established after the United States acquired Alaska from the Russian Empire in 1867. The acquisition was prompted by U.S. Secretary of State William H. Seward, and the Senate approved the transaction on April 9, 1867 for a sum of $7,200,000. The U.S. flag was raised in Alaska on October 18, 1867, an occasion now observed as Alaska Day. At the same time, the transition involved a de facto shift of the International Date Line westward and a calendar reform whereby Alaska moved from the Julian to the Gregorian system, yielding the consequence that the day following Friday, October 6, 1867 was Friday, October 18, 1867 for residents.

George Anson, 1st Baron Anson, was promoted to the rank of commander in June 1722 and given charge of the eight-gun HMS Weazel to suppress smuggling between Britain and Holland, a mission he carried out with evident efficiency. In February 1723 he advanced to post-captain and took command of the 32-gun sixth-rate HMS Scarborough, receiving orders to escort British merchant convoys from the Carolinas. His time in Charleston, South Carolina, is remembered in the Ansonborough district, which commemorates his residence and activities there.

George Anson, who would later be created the 1st Baron Anson, advanced in the Royal Navy with a lieutenant’s commission on 17 March 1716. He was assigned to the fourth-rate HMS Hampshire, serving in a Baltic Sea fleet commanded by Admiral John Norris. In March 1718 he transferred to the aging fourth-rate HMS Montagu, and in August 1718 took part in action against Spain at the Battle of Cape Passaro during the War of the Quadruple Alliance. In October 1719 he moved to the second-rate HMS Barfleur, which served as the flagship of Admiral George Byng.

Speedway LLC served as the official fuel supplier for the NTT IndyCar Series and for Indianapolis Motor Speedway, with the designation active from 2019 through 2022. The fuel specification used was E85 race fuel, continuing the formulation that had been in place since 2012. In addition, Speedway announced an endorsement agreement with Ally Ewing, a professional golfer on the LPGA Tour.

After Marathon Petroleum acquired Andeavor, company-owned stations in California that would previously have borne the Rich branding were rebranded as Speedway Express, a move designed to introduce and establish the Speedway banner in California, where the brand was new. Speedway Express accepts the Speedy Rewards loyalty card, unlike the Rich branding. Beyond California, Speedway Express locations are also present in Alaska, Oregon, and Washington, but none of the Speedway Express stores in these states operate as conventional Speedway outlets.

Within the Roman Empire, republican equality gradually eroded, producing an informal division between the honestiores and the humiliores. The honestiores encompassed members of the three higher orders and certain senior military officers. The 212 CE Constitutio Antoniniana granted universal citizenship, intensifying competition among the upper classes to demonstrate their superiority, especially within the justice system. Sentencing was influenced by the presiding official’s assessment of the defendant’s dignitas, or social worth. Consequently, an honestior could pay a fine for offenses that a humilior might receive corporal punishment for, such as scourging.

Livy, the principal Latin prose author of the Augustan age, produced a narrative of Rome’s founding that became the most familiar account in later literature. In the realm of imperial biography, Suetonius’s The Twelve Caesars stands as a central primary source for the lives of Rome’s rulers. Beyond Latin writing, Greek imperial historians such as Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Josephus, and Cassius Dio offered important perspectives on Rome’s rise and governance. Among other prominent Greek writers of the Empire, Plutarch contributed biographical sketches, Strabo provided geographic descriptions, and Lucian offered rhetorical and satirical voices. Together, these authors shaped classical understanding of Rome’s foundation, political development, imperial institutions, and cultural life.

Turnbull & Asser is a British retailer of men's apparel founded in 1885. Its flagship store is located on Jermyn Street in St James's, London, with a nearby bespoke outlet on Bury Street just around the corner from the flagship. The firm also operates a shop in New York City.

Turnbull & Asser, a British shirtmaker and tailor, rose to prominence in the 1960s by servicing the Swinging London fashion scene. In 1962 the company supplied shirts and ties for Dr. No, the inaugural film in the James Bond series. The portrayal of James Bond, played by Sean Connery, featured dress shirts with turnback cuffs secured by buttons, a style often described as cocktail cuffs or James Bond cuffs. The firm continued to provide shirts for later Bond films, including those starring Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig, reinforcing its enduring association with the franchise.

Gabriele Kröcher-Tiedemann, a member of the Red Army Faction (RAF), was arrested in Switzerland the following month, together with fellow radical Christian Möller in the Canton of Jura after crossing the border from France at Fahy. Tiedemann fired on two border guards with a pistol, and the pair fled to Porrentruy before taking a taxi to Delémont, where they were apprehended at a police roadblock. Initially, authorities believed they had captured Juliane Plambeck and Willy Peter Stoll; however, fingerprint checks confirmed the identities of Tiedemann and Möller. In Tiedemann's luggage were falsified identity papers, a report on the kidnapping and murder of Hanns Martin Schleyer, blueprints for the Israeli embassy in Belgium, two rifles, and $20,000 from the Palmers' ransom. Tiedemann was sentenced to 15 years in prison.

Gabriele Kröcher-Tiedemann (1951 – 7 October 1995) was a German far-left militant associated with Movement 2 June (J2M) and the Red Army Faction (RAF). She married Norbert Kröcher in 1971, with the marriage later ending in divorce during her imprisonment. She was released from prison in 1975 amid the events surrounding the kidnapping of Peter Lorenz. Kröcher-Tiedemann also participated in the OPEC siege. In 1977, she was arrested in Switzerland after shooting two policemen, and she remained in prison until 1991. She died in 1995.

Under the constitutional framework of Greater Lebanon, political offices were allocated according to sectarian quotas that mirrored the population's composition. The arrangement designated the presidency to a Maronite Christian, the premiership to a Sunni Muslim, and the speakership of the Chamber of Deputies to a Shia Muslim, with representation for Greek Orthodox and Druze in the cabinet. This system heightened sectarian tensions and hindered the development of a unified Lebanese national identity, while concentrating substantial power in the Maronite president, who possessed the authority to select the prime minister. Although the Chamber of Deputies possessed a theoretical legislative function, in practice the executive prepared most proposed laws, which the chamber nearly always approved. The Constitution nonetheless maintained the French high commissioner as the supreme authority, a position initially resisted by Lebanese nationalists. Three days after the Constitution’s adoption, Charles Debbas, a Greek Orthodox, was elected as Lebanon’s first president.

On 24 August 1920, French Prime Minister Alexandre Millerand informed Archbishop Khoury that Bekaa claims had been granted. Acting on instructions from the French government, General Gouraud proclaimed Lebanon’s incorporation of territory up to the summits of the Anti-Lebanon range and Mount Hermon, in a ceremony at Zahle’s Grand Kadri Hotel. The proclamation was intended to establish what would come to be known as Greater Lebanon, with the aim of securing Lebanon’s natural borders. The defined area encompassed the Bekaa Valley, the Anti-Lebanon range, and Mount Hermon.

Advancing digital technologies, especially the Internet, have reshaped the traditional function of record labels by enabling artists to distribute material online at little to no cost through channels such as online radio and BitTorrent, though these avenues often yield modest financial returns. In response, some artists have left major-label contracts when they perceived the industry as uncooperative, later returning to major-label systems to gain international marketing and promotional reach. For instance, Nine Inch Nails ended its contract with a major label and subsequently rejoined to access broader international distribution, while Radiohead released In Rainbows under a pay-what-you-want online model during its EMI deal and later returned to conventional release. Despite such shifts, research indicates that record labels still exercise substantial control over access to distribution, underscoring their ongoing central role in the music business.

Record labels and artists often navigate a relationship that can be fraught with tension, as labels aim to optimize commercial potential while artists pursue their creative aims. Disagreements over the intended sound or selected songs can lead to changes in packaging elements such as artwork or even the release title before the work reaches audiences. In some instances, material may be prevented from release or kept undistributed, effectively shelved by the label. To maximize sales, labels may push modifications that align with their market strategy, even if those changes alter the artist’s original concept. Consequently, decisions that are commercially prudent can still frustrate artists who feel that their art has been diminished or misrepresented.

Alya Rohali (born 1 December 1976) is an Indonesian film and television actress, television host, notary, model, and beauty pageant titleholder. She was crowned Puteri Indonesia in 1996 and subsequently represented Indonesia at Miss Universe 1996. Rohali is noted as the first and only person to hold the Puteri Indonesia title for four consecutive years (1996–1999), during which she served as Indonesia's representative at all major international beauty competitions.

Alya Rohali is an Indonesian television presenter and former beauty pageant titleholder who rose to prominence as the co-host of the quiz show Siapa Berani? alongside Helmy Yahya. The pair won the Panasonic Gobel Awards in 2002 in the Best Male and Female Quiz Show Host category. Rohali has been described as the most successful Indonesian beauty pageant winner to transition into the entertainment industry, moving from pageantry to television roles. She reportedly lost ten kilograms in two months and was appointed as a celebrity spokesperson for a slimming center. Rohali holds a Master of Law degree from the University of Indonesia and is a notary.

In 1956, Arthur L. Samuel at IBM's Poughkeepsie laboratory programmed an IBM 704 to play checkers and to learn from experience, a milestone widely cited as the first practical demonstration of artificial intelligence. In 1957, FORTRAN, a scientific programming language, was developed.

IBM, a leading American multinational technology company, has employed a number of individuals who later gained prominence in diverse fields. Notable former IBM employees include Michael J. Massimino, a NASA astronaut; Julie Payette, a Canadian astronaut and former Governor General of Canada; the musician Dave Matthews; Maria Klawe, president of Harvey Mudd College; Robert Mendenhall, president emeritus of Western Governors University; Lee T. Todd Jr., a former president of the University of Kentucky; Bruce Harreld, a former president of the University of Iowa; Bill Carollo, an NFL referee; John McClelland, who served as chairman of Rangers F.C.; J. M. Coetzee, a Nobel Prize in Literature laureate; and Thomas Watson Jr., the 11th national president of the Boy Scouts of America. These examples illustrate IBM's historical role in developing leaders across science, higher education, the arts, sports administration, and public life.
The next Bulgarian parliamentary elections are scheduled to be held by 11 January 2029. This timetable follows a series of snap votes conducted amid a political crisis that began in 2021.

Bulgaria experienced a period of political instability marked by several snap elections as the National Assembly repeatedly failed to form a durable government. In April 2021, anti-corruption parties emerged as notable newcomers, altering the electoral landscape. The 2023 parliamentary election followed a pattern similar to 2022, with the centre-right GERB–SDS narrowly defeating the centrist PP–DB. The vote also saw gains for the far-right Vazrazhdane and for the populist There Is Such a People, while ITN re-entered the Assembly in 2023 after failing to clear the 2022 electoral threshold.

AstroForge's inaugural orbital spacecraft, Brokkr-1, was developed and built by OrbAstro, a British satellite manufacturer. Housed in a 6U cubesat form factor, the mission is focused on demonstrating technology capable of extracting metals from asteroid materials. The payload operations involve vaporizing asteroid-like matter and separating the metallic components from other constituent materials.

AstroForge is a space resources company focused on extracting, refining, and selling platinum-group metals from M-type asteroids in the near-Earth region. The initiative targets relatively small bodies, roughly 20 to 300 meters in diameter, in contrast with the larger objects found in the main asteroid belt. M-type asteroids comprise about three to five percent of the Near-Earth Asteroid population. In its planning, AstroForge has identified five particular asteroids that meet these criteria as potential mining targets for future operations. Unlike several other space-resource ventures that prioritize harvesting water ice to support the creation of interplanetary fuel depots, AstroForge does not pursue that pathway at present, citing the absence of a currently viable market for such depots.

Across Nepal, caste- and tribe-based hierarchies are observed among the country’s diverse ethnic communities. Historically, the four-Varna model of social division did not uniformly apply to all groups, with only three communities traditionally included within this framework. These groups are the Khas/Parbatiya and the Newars in the hill regions, and the Madhesis in the plains.

The Nepalese caste system is the traditional framework of social stratification in Nepal. It largely adopts the classical Hindu model of four varnas, known as the Chaturvarnashram framework, organizing society into hierarchical groups and associated duties. The system comprises four principal varnas: Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Sudras, which have historically governed patterns of occupation, ritual status, and social interaction within Nepalese communities, though regional variations and historical change have altered their relative prominence over time.

The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints in the Solomon Islands began with the organization of its first local branch on February 4, 1996. As membership grew, additional branches were established, leading to the organization of the Honiara Solomon Islands District on November 27, 2011 to oversee the local units. By 2024, the district reported 1,627 members and comprised eight branches: Auki, Burns Creek, Fauabu Malaita, Honiara, Kola'a Ridge (Honiara), Point Cruz (Honiara), Ulawa, and White River (Honiara).

In the Solomon Islands region, the expansion of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints progressed through the migration of Tongan members to the New Hebrides (now Vanuatu) in the early 1970s. A local branch was formed in Port Vila on 15 July 1973, marking the first organized presence in the territory, which later led to the creation of the Port Vila District on 19 October 1996. The neighboring Luganville District followed, being organized on 27 September 1998, and the Port Vila Vanuatu Stake was established on 21 June 2015, with about 2,000 people in attendance. These milestones reflect the gradual development of Latter-day Saint organizational structures within the region surrounding the Solomon Islands.

Korean postpositions, or particles, function as affixes or brief units that attach directly after a noun or pronoun to mark grammatical relations. The article employs the Revised Romanization of Korean to indicate pronunciation, while the Hangul representations in the official orthography are shown beneath.

The Apache ORC format is widely supported across data processing platforms and tools. In particular, it is supported by AWS Glue, Google Cloud Platform's BigQuery, and the Pandas library, reflecting its broad interoperability within both cloud and open-source ecosystems.

Apache ORC, which stands for Optimized Row Columnar, is a free and open-source column-oriented data storage format designed for efficient analytics on large data sets. It is comparable to other columnar formats in the Hadoop ecosystem, such as RCFile and Parquet, and aims to improve storage efficiency and query performance. The format is utilized by several prominent data processing frameworks, including Apache Spark, Apache Hive, Apache Flink, and Apache Hadoop, to enable efficient ingestion, storage, and retrieval of data within complex processing pipelines.

Before May 1, 2004, the European Union consisted of fifteen member states; on that date ten new member states joined, enlarging the Union. The article documents the party affiliations of the leaders of each member state represented in the European Council during the period from January 1 to May 1, 2004. For every state, the entry identifies the head of government or head of state, their domestic political party, and the European political alliance of that party. States are listed from most to least populous, reflecting the greater influence of larger states within the European Council under the Qualified Majority Voting system.

Between January and April 2004, Greece and Spain underwent changes of government. Despite these changes, the European Council’s overall balance of party affiliations remained stable, with no net shift in the distribution of governing parties represented among the member states during this period.

In June 1838, Barry and his colleagues toured Britain to locate a suitable stone supply for the building. They selected Magnesian Limestone quarried at the Anston quarry, owned by the Duke of Leeds. Construction on the river frontage commenced on 1 January 1839, and the foundation stone was laid on 27 April 1840 by Barry's wife. The stone proved to be poorly quarried and mishandled, and London's polluted atmosphere contributed to ongoing problems. The first signs of deterioration appeared in 1849, and the structure subsequently required periodic, extensive renovations.

Following the 1834 fire that destroyed the Palace of Westminster, King William IV proposed Buckingham Palace as a temporary replacement for Parliament; however MPs rejected the offer, deeming Buckingham Palace dingy for parliamentary business. With Parliament still needing a meeting place, the Lesser Hall and Painted Chamber were both re-roofed and furnished to accommodate the Commons and Lords respectively. These arrangements made possible the State Opening of Parliament on 23 February 1835 in the modified spaces.

The island nation's Muslim community in Tonga sought to raise funds in the Middle East to construct a new boarding school on Tongatapu. The proposed facility would follow the national curriculum while offering Arabic language study and Islamic studies as optional subjects. The plan envisions a three-storey boarding house intended to serve Muslims and non-Muslims alike, with a particular emphasis on providing education for orphans who have been deprived of schooling. Participation would be voluntary, and there would be no obligation for students to study or to convert to Islam. The project is associated with Sheikh Imam Abdul Fader, described as a spiritual leader and mathematics teacher. A small delegation of Tongan Muslims was planned to travel in June 2007 to Saudi Arabia and Qatar to seek donations and funding. In this context, Saudi Arabia and Qatar are recognized for their significant contributions to Muslim communities in Australia and New Zealand.

Islam in Tonga represents a minority faith in a country that is predominantly Christian. The secular structure of Tonga’s constitution provides for freedom of religion, including the right to proselytize and to establish places of worship for Muslims. The community is largely comprised of adherents from Sunni Islam and the Ahmadiyya movement. Demographic estimates place the number of Muslims in Tonga at under 1,000, within a total population of about 108,000 (Pew Research Center, 2010). A separate estimate from the Fiji Muslim League in 2002 gave Tonga’s Muslim population at roughly 100 individuals, of whom about 70 were Tongan nationals.

The Facebook onion address refers to a Tor-accessible version of the social network intended to distinguish between accounts compromised by botnets and those accessed legitimately through Tor. At its release in 2014, the project was in an early development stage and required further refinement to ensure reliable Tor access. Analysts and commentators speculated that other companies might likewise establish their own onion services to provide Tor-enabled access to their platforms.

In October 2014, Facebook announced the launch of a Tor onion service enabling access to the social network through the Tor Browser with HTTPS encryption. Security researcher Alec Muffett described the service as preserving Tor's cryptographic protections and enabling end-to-end communication from the user's browser to a Facebook data center. The onion address used for the service was facebookcorewwwi.onion, a backronym for Facebook's Core WWW Infrastructure.

Materials are substances or combinations that constitute the components of objects and environments. They may be pure substances or impure mixtures, and they can originate from living systems as well as from non-living sources. Classification of materials can be based on physical properties such as mechanical, thermal, or other characteristics; on chemical properties including composition and reactivity; on geological origin, distinguishing natural minerals and rocks from synthetic or biologically derived sources; and on biological function, reflecting roles within living organisms. The field of materials science studies the relationships between the structure, properties, performance, and applications of materials, drawing on principles from physics, chemistry, and engineering to understand and design materials for a wide range of uses.

In foams and textiles, the properties that are immediately observable are determined primarily by macrostructural features rather than by chemical composition. The dominant large-scale characteristics are the porosity of foams and the weave of textiles, and these features largely govern attributes such as permeability, insulation, mechanical behavior, and texture. Consequently, the chemical structure tends to be of secondary importance in shaping the immediate properties of these materials.

On January 13, 2017, Natalie Hemby released her debut studio album, Puxico. The album’s title references the Missouri town where her grandfather had lived. It was issued by GetWrucke Productions, a label run by Hemby and her husband, Mike Wrucke, who is a music producer.
In February 2021, Natalie Hemby signed with Fantasy Records. Pins and Needles marked her first album for the label, was produced by Mike Wrucke, and was released on October 8, 2021.

In analyses of Plains Indian representations, a passage presents a speaker who rejects the literal assertion that only dead Indians are considered good, while contending that roughly nine out of ten Indians have already died. He further indicates no interest in examining the fate or condition of the remaining one, effectively sidelining that tenth. The passage is cited as an example of overt hostility and dehumanization directed at Plains Indians, illustrating how such rhetoric reinforced prejudicial and demeaning portrayals within settler-colonial discourse.

Across the Plains, the Lakota and other northern nomadic groups followed a seasonal cycle. The year typically began with a communal spring buffalo hunt after their horses recovered from winter, and during June or July bands gathered into large encampments where ceremonies such as the Sun Dance were held. These gatherings served as a forum for leaders to make political decisions, plan migrations, settle disputes, and organize raids or war parties. In the autumn, the population dispersed into smaller bands to focus on provisioning meat to sustain the long winter. Between the autumn hunt and winter, Lakota warriors could undertake raiding and warfare. As winter snows arrived, groups settled into winter camps, carried out seasonal ceremonies and dances, and ensured adequate fodder for their horses. On the southern Plains, milder winters often shifted raiding activity into the fall and winter months. Beginning in the 1830s, the Comanche and their allies frequently conducted deep raids into Mexico for horses and goods, sometimes traveling about 1,000 miles (1,600 km) south from the Red River region in Texas and Oklahoma.

The Respect for Marriage Act earned backing from more than forty faith-based organizations, reflecting broad religious endorsement of the measure. Many of these groups permit same‑sex marriages within their traditions and affirm LGBT parishioners, and they collectively submitted a joint letter to the Senate in support of the legislation. Notable endorsing bodies include the Episcopal Church; the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America; Hindus for Human Rights; the Interfaith Alliance; Jewish Women International; Muslims for Progressive Values; the National Council of Jewish Women; the Presbyterian Church (USA); the Reconstructionist Rabbinical Association; the Religious Action Center of Reform Judaism; the Sikh Coalition; the Union for Reform Judaism; the Unitarian Universalist Association; and the United Church of Christ.

Respect for Marriage Act (RFMA) is federal legislation intended to codify nationwide recognition of same‑sex marriages. It replaced the Defense of Marriage Act’s interpretation that the Full Faith and Credit Clause did not require states to recognize same‑sex marriages performed in other states. In United States v. Windsor (2013), the Supreme Court struck down that portion of DOMA. After the Dobbs decision overturned Roe v. Wade, concerns emerged that Windsor could be overturned in the future. The RFMA substituted the DOMA provision with language affirming that the Full Faith and Credit Clause requires interstate recognition of valid same‑sex marriages. Consequently, the act ensures nationwide recognition of same‑sex marriages across all states.
Unicode assigns braille characters to the general category So (Symbol, other), rather than Lo (Letter, other). In the ISO 15924 standard, the Braille script is designated by the code Brai.

Within the Unicode standard, braille patterns are named using the plural form "dots" in their identifiers, such as "braille pattern dots-5," even when describing a single raised dot. By contrast, everyday English usage typically refers to a lone raised cell as "braille dot 5" or simply "dot 5." This difference highlights a divergence between formal encoding terminology and colloquial speech.

During the spring of 312, Constantine led about 40,000 troops, roughly a quarter of his forces, across the Alps by the Mont Cenis pass through the Cottian range and reached Segusium (Susa, Italy), a strongly fortified town whose garrison closed its gates. After directing the gates to be burned and the walls scaled, Segusium fell swiftly. He subsequently forbade the plunder of the captured town, and, secure in this victory, advanced further into northern Italy.

Maxentius co-governed Rome with Maximian, a rule that was challenged when Galerius invaded Italy in the summer of 307. He exploited monetary promises and Maximian's authority to induce defections among Galerius's troops, prompting Galerius to withdraw while plundering parts of Italy on his retreat. During the campaign, Severus was killed by Maxentius, probably at Tres Tabernae near Rome, though the exact circumstances remain uncertain. Following the failure of Galerius's expedition, Maxentius solidified his authority over Italy and Africa. From 307 onward, he sought closer, more outwardly friendly ties with Constantine. In that summer, Maximian moved to Gaul; at roughly the same time Constantine married Fausta and was proclaimed Augustus by the senior emperor. Nevertheless, Constantine attempted to avoid breaking with Galerius and did not openly back Maxentius during the invasion.

Facebook, along with other emerging social networks such as Twitter, connected hundreds of millions of users and reshaped political communication. By 2008, politicians and interest groups were experimenting with systematic use of social media to disseminate messages, and by the 2016 election, targeted political advertising had become a normalized practice, with Facebook offering the most advanced targeting and analytics capabilities among major platforms. An early example involved more than a million people installing the Facebook app labeled "US Politics on Facebook" to participate in measuring responses to comments during candidate debates. In assessments of its electoral impact, a CBS News/UWIRE/The Chronicle of Higher Education poll attributed a "Facebook effect" to higher youth voting rates, greater support for candidates, and increased overall involvement. Nevertheless, investigations such as ProPublica highlighted concerns about micro-targeting, noting that the system enabled advertisers to direct pitches to nearly 2,300 users who had expressed interest in antisemitic or hate-related topics.

Facebook has faced ongoing privacy controversies and has repeatedly revised its privacy settings and policies in response. Since 2009, Facebook has participated in the PRISM program, sharing data from user profiles with the United States National Security Agency, including audio, video, photographs, emails, documents, and connection logs, among other content. This data sharing occurs alongside other social media services.

Angel is a London Underground station located in the Angel area of the London Borough of Islington. It lies on the Bank branch of the Northern line, positioned between King's Cross St Pancras and Old Street stations, and is in fare zone 1. The station was constructed by the City and South London Railway and opened on 17 November 1901, initially serving as the line's terminus until the extension to Euston was completed on 12 May 1907.

Angel is a London Underground station on the Bank/City branch of the Northern line in fare zone 1. It is located between King's Cross St Pancras to the north and Old Street to the south. Train frequencies on this route typically range from three to six minutes, and services operate in both directions from around 05:50 until 00:40.
In August 2018, Maroon 5 was ranked 37th on Billboard's Hot 100 60th Anniversary Greatest of All Time list and 11th on Billboard's list of the top 60 duos and groups of all time.

Maroon 5 transitioned from A&M Octone Records to Interscope Records in May 2014, in collaboration with Adam Levine's imprint 222 Records. The band announced its fifth studio album, V (pronounced “five”), which was released on September 2, 2014, in a limited-edition ZinePak packaging. The lead single “Maps” was issued on June 16, 2014, and peaked at number six on the Billboard Hot 100. The group headlined the Hyundai Card City Break festival in South Korea on August 10, 2014, and then performed at the 2014 MTV Video Music Awards on August 24, delivering live versions of “Maps” and “One More Night.” The second single, “Animals,” followed on August 25, 2014 and reached number three on the Hot 100, with the track later featuring in Kia’s 2015 Soul EV commercial.

The National Property Board of Sweden (SFV) administers a portion of the state's real property assets. Its portfolio comprises more than 2,300 properties, totaling approximately 4,300 buildings. The properties encompass a wide range of types, including castles, museums, theatres, historic fortifications, ministry buildings, embassies, county residences, and parks.

Established in 1993, the National Property Board of Sweden (SFV) originated from the division of the former National Board of Public Building (Byggnadsstyrelsen) into several specialized agencies, including Akademiska Hus, Vasakronan, and SFV. SFV subsequently assumed responsibility for a portion of the state’s real estate portfolio, a collection that largely consisted of buildings of historical value. The properties under SFV’s care required careful long-term management to preserve their heritage and ensure their continued use.

Leaflet originated in 2010 as a project known as Web Maps API for the CloudMade mapping provider. At that time, Vladimir Agafonkin was employed by CloudMade and contributed to the effort. In May 2011, CloudMade announced the first release of Leaflet. The inaugural version was developed from scratch, while reusing portions of the code from the previous API.

Leaflet provides built-in support for several layer types, notably Web Map Service (WMS) layers, GeoJSON layers, vector layers, and tile layers. Its architecture permits the addition of further layer types through plugins, enabling extended functionality beyond the core set.

Birmingham has a temperate maritime climate (Cfb), aligning with much of the British Isles and characterized by relatively mild summers and cool winters. The average daily maximum temperature in July is 21.3°C, while in January the average maximum is 6.7°C. During the period 1971–2000, the warmest day on average reaches 28.8°C, and the coldest night typically falls to around −9.0°C. Approximately 11.2 days per year experience maxima of 25.1°C or higher, and about 51.6 nights per year see air frost. Record high temperatures were observed on 19 July 2022, with 37.4°C recorded at the Edgbaston Campus and 37.0°C at Birmingham Airport.

Birmingham has a long-standing educational tradition, evidenced by historic institutions such as King Edward's School, Birmingham, which traces its origins to 1552 when it was founded by King Edward VI and ranks among the city's oldest schools. The school provides GCSEs and the International Baccalaureate, and its alumni include J. R. R. Tolkien, the author of The Lord of the Rings and The Hobbit. The city also hosts several independent schools, including Birmingham Blue Coat School, King Edward VI High School for Girls, and Edgbaston High School for Girls. In addition, Bishop Vesey's Grammar School, established in 1527 by Bishop Vesey, forms part of Birmingham's historic scholastic landscape.

Cache invalidation is a mechanism that promptly removes cached content from a caching proxy to prevent the continued serving of stale data. When the next client request arrives, the system retrieves the current data from the application server, and the retrieved data is subsequently stored in the caching proxy for future requests.
