Gas turbine power plants convert the energy of the flowing air and the exhaust gases into rotational energy to drive the turbine directly. They are typically fueled by natural gas, although oil-fueled variants are also used. Their ability to start rapidly makes them well suited for supplying peak power during periods of high demand. Compared with base-load plants, gas turbine units generally incur higher operating costs. These facilities are often comparatively compact and can be operated unmanned or remotely. The technology was developed in the United Kingdom, with Princetown hosting the world’s first installation, commissioned in 1959.

Zénobe Gramme, a Belgian inventor, developed a generator in early 1871 that proved capable of delivering power on a commercial scale for industrial use. This advancement demonstrated the viability of large‑scale electricity production and helped pave the way for the emergence of power plants as central facilities for supplying industry.

Matt Walker is a drummer who has performed as Morrissey's drummer since 2006. He appears on Morrissey's albums Years of Refusal, Swords, World Peace Is None of Your Business, Low in High School, and I Am Not a Dog on a Chain.

Matt Walker is an American drummer who has contributed to notable projects in the alternative rock scene. In 2005 he played drums on Garbage's Bleed Like Me, helping to shape the album's rhythm section. He later worked with Billy Corgan, recording material and touring to promote the solo album TheFutureEmbrace.

Absolutely Fabulous uses This Wheel's on Fire as its theme song, a composition credited to Bob Dylan and Rick Danko and originally performed by Julie Driscoll and Adrian Edmondson, Saunders' Comic Strip colleague and later husband. The track has since been presented by a range of artists across the series and its specials, including Marianne Faithfull and P. P. Arnold in the 1996 two-part special The Last Shout; in the 2001 Series 4 episode Paris, the closing credits feature Hermine Demoriane singing with a French accent; at the end of Series 1's Birthday, Edina and Patsy perform it on a karaoke machine; in the 2002 Christmas special Gay, Debbie Harry performs it with Edmondson, with Harry guest-starring, and the song also appears in Series 5; and in Series 4, the end credits incorporate a line from David Bowie's Ziggy Stardust.

On 3 January 2012, speculation emerged that Jennifer Saunders would write a Christmas special for 2012 in response to the success of the 20th anniversary specials. Concurrent reports suggested that the BBC was encouraging her to develop a sixth series for a 2013 release. Saunders subsequently denied these accounts, announcing via Twitter that there were no plans for additional episodes.

Say is a song by John Mayer. Billboard’s Chuck Taylor described the track as a lilting, bittersweet ballad, and he suggested it was likely to become another staple on the adult contemporary radio format.

Say is a song by American singer-songwriter John Mayer. The track received the Grammy Award for Best Male Pop Vocal Performance at the 51st Annual Grammy Awards in 2009, and it was also nominated for Best Song Written for a Motion Picture, Television or Other Visual Media.

In May 2010, the supplementary sheets linked to DIN EN 61346 were withdrawn, namely IEC/TR 61346-3:2001, which provided application guidelines, and IEC 61346-4:1998, which addressed terms and their relationships. The withdrawal occurred without the release of any replacement material.

IEC 81346 designates a set of reference designation and marking standards that, beginning in 2010, are to be issued as a standard developed collaboratively by the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) and the International Organization for Standardization (ISO). These standards are planned for publication within the 80000 numerical series, and the formal designation assigned to them is 81346.

Composite endpoints combine several clinically important outcomes into a single measure. In studies of myocardial infarction, the endpoint may encompass events such as chest pain, myocardial infarction, or death. In oncology trials, disease-free survival functions as a composite endpoint defined by death or the occurrence of any recurrence. Additionally, Overall Treatment Utility represents a multidimensional composite endpoint employed in cancer clinical trials.

Duration of response is a clinical endpoint used to evaluate treatment benefit in advanced disease. The event of interest is disease progression or relapse after an initial response. The analysis involves identifying the subset of patients who have responded, and then measuring how long that response lasts within that group. Non-responders are excluded from the evaluation, so the measure specifically reflects the durability of response among those who responded rather than the overall response rate across all patients.

Central Cardamom Mountains National Park spans three provinces in southwestern Cambodia. On its eastern side, it is flanked by Phnom Aural Wildlife Sanctuary, while on its western side, it is flanked by Phnom Samkos Wildlife Sanctuary.

Central Cardamom Mountains National Park is a protected area located in the central Cardamom Mountains of Cambodia. It covers 4,013.13 square kilometers (1,549.48 square miles) and was established in 1999 as a protected forest, initially under the administration of the Forestry Administration. In 2016, stewardship of the park was transferred to the Ministry of Environment, which has since overseen its conservation and management.

On August 29, 2021, Hurricane Ida struck Louisiana, making its landfall near Port Fourchon as a powerful cyclone. The storm reached the upper end of Category 4 intensity, with maximum sustained winds around 150 mph. The landfall coincided with the 16th anniversary of Hurricane Katrina’s landfall in Louisiana. Ida contributed to 33 fatalities and generated insured losses of at least $18 billion across the state.

Between August 5 and 7, 2002, Tropical Storm Bertha brushed the Louisiana coast, making landfall near Boothville as a minimal tropical storm with winds around 40 mph (64 km/h) and a central pressure of 1,008 mb (29.8 inHg). The system traversed Louisiana as it weakened, later re-entering the Gulf of Mexico on August 7. Rainfall was scattered across the state, with a peak total of 10.25 inches (26.0 cm) recorded southwest of Franklinton. Flooding affected several areas, including flooded streets in Slidell, while runoff in St. Tammany Parish caused some rivers to rise above flood stage. Overall, the damage in Louisiana was estimated at $150,000 in 2002 dollars (approximately $260,000 in 2024 dollars).

Wendell Marshall was an American jazz double bassist notable for his long association with Duke Ellington's orchestra. A cousin of bassist Jimmy Blanton, he studied with Blanton and inherited Blanton's bass after Blanton's death. Marshall attended Sumner High School and pursued further studies at Lincoln University. In 1942 he briefly played with Lionel Hampton before serving in the United States Army from 1943 to 1946. After his discharge, he performed with Jimmy Forrest, Buggs Roberts, and Stuff Smith, before moving to New York City where he worked with Mercer Ellington. He joined Duke Ellington's band, performing with the ensemble from 1948 to 1955, and made his Carnegie Hall debut with the group on November 13, 1948.

Wendell Marshall was an American jazz double bassist who began his career after his tenure with Duke Ellington by joining Broadway pit orchestras. On Broadway, he contributed to shows including Fiddler on the Roof and A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum. As a freelance musician, he worked with Mary Lou Williams, Art Blakey, Donald Byrd, Milt Jackson, Hank Jones, and other notable artists. In 1955–56 he was part of Savoy Records’ house rhythm section, alongside Hank Jones and Kenny Clarke. Across his recording career, Marshall appeared on more than 370 sessions. He released only one record as a leader, the album Wendell Marshall and the Billy Byers Orchestra.

Maxfield Frederick Parrish studied at the Drexel Institute, where he met his future wife, Lydia Ambler Austin, a drawing teacher. They married on June 1, 1895, and relocated to Philadelphia, where the couple raised four children. In 1898, Parrish moved with his family to Plainfield, New Hampshire, where he built a home nicknamed “The Oaks.” The residence and an adjacent studio were set amid landscapes that served as inspiration for his drawings.

In 1986, Nestlé released a television advertisement for its Alpine White chocolate bar titled "Sweet Dreams," which staged live-action representations of Maxfield Parrish's paintings Ecstasy, Dinky Bird, and Daybreak.
Zhořec is a municipality and village in the Pelhřimov District of the Vysočina Region in the Czech Republic, and it has approximately 100 inhabitants.
Zhořec lies about 19 km (12 mi) west of Pelhřimov, about 46 km (29 mi) west of Jihlava, and about 78 km (48 mi) southeast of Prague.

Schroders, a British financial services company, advanced its corporate structure in 1959 when J. Henry Schroder & Co. Ltd issued its shares publicly on the London Stock Exchange. In 1962, the group broadened its investment banking capabilities through the acquisition of Helbert, Wagg & Co., a leading issuing house.

Schroders plc appointed Chris Durack and Karine Szenberg as co-heads of its client groups in 2023, a move that formed part of an internal restructuring aimed at driving growth. The initiative focused on expanding across the Asia-Pacific region.

Wallemiomycetes is a class within the Basidiomycota that comprises a single order, Wallemiales, a single family, Wallemiaceae, and the genus Wallemia. Its precise phylogenetic placement within Basidiomycota has varied, but analyses incorporating larger datasets converge on its being a sister lineage to the Agaricomycotina. The genus consists of xerophilic molds with a global distribution and includes seven described species: W. sebi, W. ichthyophaga, W. muriae, W. mellicola, W. canadensis, W. tropicalis, and W. hederae. Species are distinguished by differences in conidial size, tolerance to desiccation and salt, responsiveness to chaotropic conditions, growth temperature ranges, profiles of extracellular enzyme activities, and patterns of secondary metabolites. They are commonly recovered from low-moisture environments such as baked goods (cakes and bread), sugars, peanuts, and dried fish, as well as from indoor air dust, salterns, and soil. W. sebi has been implicated as a cause of hypersensitivity pneumonitis, known as farmer's lung, although the involvement of other Wallemia species has not yet been fully ruled out following their recent separation from W. sebi.

Wallemiomycetes constitute a small class of fungi characterized by notable tolerance to desiccation and osmotic stress. In general, the ability to endure low water activity is more common among ascomycetous lineages than among basidiomycetous ones. Xerotolerant fungi can grow on ordinary growth media with typical water activity, a contrast to halophilic Archaea that require highly saline conditions. The genus Wallemia stands as an exception to both patterns, with species that tolerate substantial concentrations of sugars and salts. In particular, Wallemia ichthyophaga can thrive in environments saturated with sodium chloride, although cultivation of W. muriae and W. ichthyophaga on standard media necessitates lowering the medium’s water activity.

The Ministry of Justice of Saudi Arabia (Arabic: وزارة العدل) is a government agency established in 1970 by King Faisal. It oversees the court system and prosecutorial services and manages their financial and administrative requirements, while also being responsible for appointing judges and licensing attorneys, translators, and other legal professionals. In the Global Competitiveness Report 2019, Saudi Arabia was ranked 16th worldwide in judicial independence, an improvement of eight places from the previous year; the efficiency of the legal framework for dispute resolution was placed 17th globally, up four positions; the harmonization of the legal framework for digital business remained 11th; and the efficiency of the legal framework for challenging regulations was ranked 18th globally, rising by 11 places.
By 2020, the Ministry of Justice of Saudi Arabia had aligned itself with the Saudi Transformation Program, setting a target to digitalize approximately 80% of its services.

In 1985, Queen Elizabeth II undertook a royal visit to Antigua and Barbuda. During the visit she met patients and staff in the newly established Children's Ward at Holberton Hospital, highlighting the monarch’s engagement with local health services. The tour followed the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting held in the Bahamas, connecting the visit to broader Commonwealth affairs.

During 2006, the Earl of Wessex undertook a royal visit to Antigua and Barbuda to represent the Queen on the 25th anniversary of the nation's independence. The programme commenced on 30 October with his participation in a Joint Sitting of Parliament at the newly built Parliament Building in Saint John's. On 31 October, he visited the Salvation Army Sunshine Home for Girls and the Boys Training School at Comfort Hall in Saint John's. On 1 November, he represented the Queen at the Independence Parade at Government House in Saint John's and attended the Independence Day Reception at Government House, the Independence Day Food Fair, and the gala dinner commemorating the twenty-fifth anniversary of independence at the Grand Royal Antiguan Hotel, also in Saint John's. The tour concluded on 2 November with a reception at Codrington Wharf in Barbuda and a luncheon with the Barbuda Council at the Beach House Hotel.

Market Identifier Codes (MICs) are subject to regular updates. The most recent MIC roster is issued by the ISO 10383 maintenance organization. The MIC list is made available in multiple formats, including Excel, CSV, XML, and PDF. It encompasses entries that have been modified and those that have been deactivated. To accompany each release, change lists are provided detailing the differences from the preceding update.

Market Identifier Code (MIC) is a standardized coding system defined under ISO 10383 that identifies exchanges, trading platforms, and markets—whether regulated or unregulated—as sources of prices and related information to support automated processing. In the FIX Protocol, MICs are used to encode values of the Fix Exchange data type, enabling consistent representation of trading venues across systems. Markets across asset classes, including equities, options, and futures, obtain MICs through the ISO framework, ensuring a uniform method for designation and data interchange.

In November 2015, Atos announced its plan to acquire Unify, the software company then owned by The Gores Group and Siemens, in a deal valued at €340 million. The transaction was completed in January 2016.

In March 2002, Siemens Communications reorganized into two primary business units. The first unit oversaw public mobile networks and fixed-network infrastructure, while the second unit concentrated on enterprise networks.

VH1 HD, launched in 2005, provides a 1080i high-definition feed of VH1. It is carried by all major providers. As of 2016, the HD feed is downgraded at the provider headend to deliver the standard-definition VH1 channel on certain systems.

VH1 MegaHits was a programming block on VH1 that showcased a curated selection of top-40 adult contemporary music videos drawn from the network’s archive, spanning the 1980s through the early 2000s. The block was discontinued due to low viewership. Subsequently, MTV Networks repurposed the satellite space formerly used for VH1 MegaHits to launch Logo in 2005, an LGBTQ-focused channel.

Renaissance humanism refers to a scholarly and cultural movement in Europe roughly from the 14th to the 17th century that revived classical Latin and Greek literature and placed emphasis on education and civic virtue. Garin argued that the humanist philosophers should function as organic intellectuals within society rather than form a rigid, insular school of thought. Despite diverse affiliations, practitioners of humanism shared a common outlook on life and learning, stressing humane studies, critical inquiry, and personal development. This orientation marked a break with medieval traditions that had previously governed intellectual life, signaling a shift toward secular, human-centered approaches to knowledge and culture.

Within Renaissance humanism, some thinkers linked the pursuit of a harmonious, agreeable life with Epicureanism, arguing that the truly righteous and devout embody Epicurean ideals. In this framework, epikouros, meaning “helper,” was invoked to portray Christ as the supreme Epicurean in name, and as the founder or head of Christian philosophy. Proponents maintained that Christ arrived as timely aid when nature’s law seemed obscured by sin, when the Mosaic Law provoked rather than healed, and when Satan purportedly ruled unchecked. They rejected claims that Christ was sad or that life should be gloomy, contending instead that Christ alone demonstrates the most enjoyable life and true pleasure.

% Arabica is a coffee brand that utilizes bespoke espresso machines designed specifically for its operations and manufactured in Seattle. The equipment affords baristas greater control over extraction parameters, including time, temperature, and pressure, enabling precise crafting of beverages. These machines underpin the brand's emphasis on artisanal drinks and specialty coffee experiences.

% Arabica is a coffee shop brand that opened its first United States location in Dumbo, Brooklyn, on June 11, 2021. The majority of its locations operate as franchises, whereas the three outlets in Kyoto are managed directly by the corporate entity.
Tereanini is recognized as one of the great ocean-going voyaging canoes (waka) in Māori tradition, and it was used in the migrations that settled New Zealand.

Tereanini was captained by Rongomaituaho, a figure described in traditional accounts as having followed his father Paikea from Hawaiki. Paikea is recognised as a principal ancestor of Ngāti Porou, and these genealogical connections form part of the tribe’s ancestral narrative preserved in oral history.

In linguistics, tautologies in ordinary language are typically unintentional, arising when two terms with overlapping meanings are paired. Common illustrations include phrases that blend mental processes with telepathic ability, descriptions of conspiracies as if they were planned, and references to dwarfs described as small. These formulations imply the existence of contrary qualities, such as a physical form of telepathy, conspiracies that occur spontaneously, or dwarfs of considerable size. Consequently, such expressions are regarded as oxymorons, defined by the juxtaposition of contradictory terms.

Tautology in language is the intentional repetition of meaning to amplify or emphasize a significant fact about the topic under discussion. It is used to underscore or reinforce a point in communication. A typical example is the phrase “free gift,” which signals that there are no hidden conditions or fine print, or that the gift is extended voluntarily. A related instance is the statement that “a gift is, by definition, free of charge,” which shows tautology through the inherent sense of the terms involved.

Andrew Marvell died suddenly in 1678 while attending a popular meeting of his old Hull constituents. Although his health had been notably good, allegations of poisoning by political or clerical enemies circulated but remain unproven. He was buried in the church of St Giles in the Fields in central London. Kingston-upon-Hull erected a monument bearing a long inscription that praises him as endowed by Nature, refined by Education, Study, and Travel, and perfected by Experience. The inscription credits him with combining wit and learning with penetrating and strong judgment, and with steadiness in the ways of Virtue. He is depicted as an ornament and example of his age, beloved by good, feared by bad, admired by all, though imitated by few, scarcely paralleled by any. A tombstone is said to be insufficient to contain his character, which, the inscription notes, is engraved in the minds of his generation and in his writings. He served twenty years in Parliament with Wisdom, Dexterity, and Courage, as a true Patriot, well-regarded by Kingston-upon-Hull. The town lamented his death and in 1688 erected the monument as an expression of their grief and gratitude.

Andrew Marvell entered Trinity College, Cambridge at the age of thirteen and subsequently earned a Bachelor of Arts degree. A portrait attributed to Godfrey Kneller depicting Marvell is held in the collection of Trinity College.

The Economist is widely regarded as a magazine, although it has traditionally described itself as a newspaper rather than a news magazine. In 1971, the publication changed its physical format from a broadsheet to a compact, perfect-binding edition. Despite the shift in presentation, it continued to identify itself as a newspaper. The magazine’s website notes that by the time the format transformation was completed, the habit of referring to itself as a newspaper had already become established.

In 2015, The Economist established a dedicated data-journalism division comprising data journalists, visualisers, and interactive developers to lead the publication’s data reporting. The team has developed election forecasting models for several contests, including France’s presidential elections in 2017 and 2022 and the United States’ presidential and congressional elections in 2020, among others. In late 2023, the data team advertised for a political data scientist to bolster political forecasting. To promote transparency, The Economist maintains a corporate GitHub account where models and software are publicly disclosed. From October 2018 to November 2023, Graphic Detail was introduced, featuring large charts and maps across print and digital editions.

Arouet adopted the name Voltaire in 1718 after his confinement in the Bastille. The precise origins of the pseudonym remain uncertain. A commonly cited theory posits that Voltaire is an anagram of AROVET LI, formed by the Latinized spelling of his surname and the initials of le jeune. Family tradition records that as a child he was known as le petit volontaire, a designation he later revived in the form Voltaire. Some accounts also suggest that the name echoes the reversal of Airvault, the Poitou hometown of his family.

Voltaire, the prominent French Enlightenment writer, has been commemorated in a number of places and through various eponyms. In 1878 the town of Ferney was renamed Ferney-Voltaire to honor him, reflecting his residence there for the last two decades of his life; his château at Ferney is today a museum dedicated to his legacy. Voltaire's library is preserved intact in the National Library of Russia in Saint Petersburg. In Zürich, in 1916, the theatre group that would become Dada named their venue Cabaret Voltaire. A late-20th-century industrial music group later adopted the same name. In astronomy, Voltaire's name was given to the Voltaire crater on Deimos and to the asteroid 5676 Voltaire, both designated in his honor.

Ramparts encompass a range of defensive earthworks, from simple dump ramparts consisting of earth-and-stone mounds to more elaborate earth-and-timber barriers. Among the more complex forms are box ramparts and timberlaced ramparts, which incorporate timber elements within the earthen core for additional strength and stability. Some ramparts are reinforced by stone revetments to improve durability against attack or weathering. In Central Europe, the Pfostenschlitzmauer, or post-slot wall, exemplifies a regional variant that combines earth, stone, and wooden posts to create a sturdy barrier. Vitrified ramparts are stone ramparts that have been fired to increase their strength, a technique intended to bind the materials and enhance defensive performance.

In fortifications, a casemate is a vaulted chamber integrated within the rampart that provides protected accommodation or storage for defenders and their equipment. The front of the casemate is sometimes pierced by an embrasure, an opening through which a firearm can be fired, allowing the weapon to cover the exterior while the occupants enjoy protection from the surrounding earthworks.

Algeria maintains an active role within the United Nations system, participating in its principal organs and mechanisms, including the Human Rights Council. The country pursues domestic and international initiatives aimed at promoting gender equality, reducing poverty, and expanding access to education. However, its domestic human rights record has attracted scrutiny, with particular concerns raised about freedom of expression and the right to peaceful assembly. Through its UN membership, Algeria has committed to multiple international human rights treaties and conventions, reflecting engagement with universal norms and reporting obligations.

Algeria joined the United Nations on 8 October 1962, shortly after gaining independence from France. It did not participate in the body's founding in 1945, as it was then part of the French colonial empire. Since acceding to membership, Algeria has been active in decolonization efforts, peacekeeping, and advocacy for non-alignment in international affairs. It participates in United Nations General Assembly sessions and has contributed personnel to several UN peacekeeping missions. The country supports initiatives aimed at advancing the rights of developing nations. Algeria's engagement with the UN is consistent with its foreign policy objectives of preserving sovereignty, supporting anti-colonial movements, and fostering cooperation across Africa and the Arab world.

During the siege of Constantinople in 717–718, the Umayyad campaign consumed a substantial portion of the Caliphate’s manpower and resources, yet it continued to permit incursions into the Byzantine frontier in eastern Asia Minor throughout the period. In 717, Daud, son of Caliph Sulayman, captured a fortress near Melitene, signaling the operational reach of the assault on frontier lines. The following year, 718, saw Amr ibn Qais conduct a raid along the frontier. The precise size of the Byzantine forces defending these eastern defenses remains unknown. Although defensive preparations under Anastasius II existed, they may have been neglected after his deposition. The Byzantines also received assistance from the Bulgar ruler Tervel, and Leo III later concluded a treaty with Tervel, which possibly included an agreement against the Arabs.

Although the siege of Constantinople (717–718) failed to topple the Byzantine capital, the expedition weakened the Umayyad Caliphate significantly, imposing financial strain and destroying Syria’s fleet and army, thereby depriving it of its principal power base. Caliph Umar reportedly weighed withdrawing from Hispania and Transoxiana and even evacuating Cilicia and other Byzantine-held territories, though his advisers urged him to persist. As a result, most Arab garrisons were withdrawn from the Byzantine frontier districts, with only Mopsuestia in Cilicia remaining as a defensive bulwark for Antioch. The aftermath saw the Byzantines temporarily recover some territory in western Armenia. In 719, the Byzantine fleet conducted a raid along the Syrian coast and burned Laodicea, and around 720 or 721 Byzantine forces attacked and sacked Tinnis in Egypt. Concurrently, Leo III restored Byzantine control over Sicily, where Basil Onomagoulos had proclaimed himself emperor, although by this period Byzantines no longer maintained effective control over Sardinia and Corsica.

Taichung line, a railway line operated by Taiwan Railways Administration in central Taiwan, is commonly referred to as the Mountain line. In Chinese, it is written 臺中線 or 台中線, with 山線 serving as the Mountain line designation. Its romanizations include pinyin Táizhōng Xiàn and Pe̍h-ōe-jī: Tâi-tiong Soàⁿ for the main line, and Shān Xiàn with Pe̍h-ōe-jī Soaⁿ-sòaⁿ for the Mountain line. The route represents one of two parallel corridors in central Taiwan and traverses inland areas as well as downtown Taichung. The total length is 85.5 kilometers (53.1 miles), and the entire line is double-tracked.

The Taichung line underwent notable modernization, with the Fengyuan–Daqing section rebuilt as an elevated alignment in 2016, and subsequently, five new stations were introduced along the route in 2018: Lilin, Toujiacuo, Songzhu, Jingwu, and Wuquan, expanding access within the corridor.

Opus 24: Rome, from the Campagna, Sunset is a landscape painting by Moran. The work is first known to have been sold in the 1880s, when Moran sold it for $75, an amount equivalent to roughly $2,444 in 2024 dollars. In 2005, a relative of the original buyer donated the painting to the Timken Museum of Art in San Diego.

"Opus 24: Rome, from the Campagna, Sunset" is an 1867 oil painting on canvas by Thomas Moran. It is one of forty-two paintings Moran included on his "Opus List," a catalog of his perceived finest works.

The Republic of Iraq is a country located in West Asia, commonly described as part of the Middle East. It is bordered by Saudi Arabia to the south, Turkey to the north, Iran to the east, the Persian Gulf and Kuwait to the southeast, Jordan to the southwest, and Syria to the west. Covering 438,317 square kilometers (169,235 square miles), Iraq ranks as the 58th-largest nation by area and is among the world’s most populous, with a population of over 46 million people, ranking 31st in population. Its capital and largest city is Baghdad, which has more than eight million residents.

Iraq preserves a Mesopotamian heritage that influenced a wide range of Old World civilizations, including the development of writing systems, mathematical thought, timekeeping, calendrical systems, astrology, and codified legal codes. The country is home to diverse ethnic communities that contribute to its rich cultural heritage. It has produced poets, architects, painters, and sculptors who are regarded as among the region’s finest, with several achieving international recognition. Iraq also has a tradition of high-quality handicrafts, notably the production of rugs and carpets.

In March 2024, the government of President Javier Milei suspended the operations of Télam, Argentina's state-owned news agency. The organization reportedly served about 300 subscribers, including government entities and national and international media outlets. Milei characterized the agency as a Kirchnerist propaganda outlet. Reported losses stood at AR$20 billion (approximately US$23 million), and at the time of the suspension the agency employed around 750 people.

During this period, Télam continued to operate as an advertising agency despite the Menem administration's plan to remove that function. In 2000, President Fernando de la Rúa announced the closure of the advertising division and the sale of Télam's headquarters, but the measures were not carried out. In 2001, the state's news media outlets were merged, and Télam was integrated with public television Canal 7 and public radio LRA Radio Nacional within the Servicio Nacional de Medios Públicos (National Service of Public Media). The following year, 2002, the modification was reversed and Télam regained its autonomy.

Deutsche Welle (DW) distributes its television programming through a network of satellite channels and carries the signal on cable networks to reach international audiences. In addition to broadcast distribution, DW provides a live stream on its website and in the ARD media library. Since 2019, DW has offered its websites as Tor onion services in order to circumvent censorship by non-democratic states.

DW Akademie offers a journalism traineeship that runs for 18 months and is designed for early-career journalists. The program targets young professionals and provides editorial training across DW’s three principal media: radio, television, and online. It is open to aspiring journalists from Germany as well as from regions where Deutsche Welle broadcasts, reflecting the organization’s international reach.

Christianity originated in the Levant and, during the early Roman Empire, spread to Europe, North Africa, and the Horn of Africa. Over time, Christendom divided into the Greek East and the Latin West, giving rise to distinct Christian cultures with their own rites and practices. Western or Latin Christendom developed around Rome and Carthage, while Eastern or Oriental Christendom centered on Constantinople, Antioch, Alexandria, Kerala, and other communities. The Byzantine Empire is regarded as a high point in Christian history and civilization. From the eleventh to the thirteenth centuries, Latin Christendom rose to a central role in the Western world and in Western cultural life.

Estimates from the Pew Research Center indicate that there were about 2.3 billion Christians worldwide in 2011, a figure that had risen markedly from roughly 600 million in 1910. Geographically, Christians are distributed with about 37 percent in the Americas, 26 percent in Europe, 24 percent in sub-Saharan Africa, 13 percent in the Asia-Pacific region, and roughly 1 percent in the Middle East and North Africa. They constitute the majority in 158 countries and territories, while around 280 million Christians live as adherents in the minority. In terms of denominational composition, Catholicism accounts for about half of Christians, with roughly 37 percent identifying as Protestant, and about 12 percent belonging to Eastern Christian traditions (including Orthodox, Oriental Orthodox, and the Church of the East), with the remainder comprising other groups. Projections from Pew suggest the Christian population could exceed 3 billion by 2050 due to comparatively higher fertility, and a 2012 Pew analysis concluded that Christianity would remain the world's largest religion in 2050 if current trends continued. Christians have faced persecution in recent history, notably in parts of the Middle East, North Africa, East Asia, and South Asia.

During 1944, Associate Justice Frank Murphy became the first Supreme Court justice to introduce the term "racism" into the Court's opinions, notably in his dissent in Korematsu v. United States (323 U.S. 214 (1944)). On that same day, he employed the word twice more in a concurring opinion in Steele v. Louisville & Nashville Railway Co. (323 U.S. 192 (1944)). Across his tenure, Murphy used "racism" in five separate Supreme Court opinions. After his departure from the Court, the term did not reappear in a Court opinion for roughly two decades, with its next appearance occurring in Loving v. Virginia (388 U.S. 1 (1967)).

The origin of the term Jim Crow is uncertain, though most scholars link it to a minstrel song and dance known as Jump Jim Crow, performed in blackface by Thomas D. Rice in 1828. The routine quickly influenced a wide range of white minstrel performers who adapted the act for white audiences, contributing to its popularity in the antebellum era and helping make Jim Crow a recognizable fixture in American popular culture. In the 1840s, abolitionists described segregated railroad cars using the phrase, and by the end of the nineteenth century the term had come to denote the social separation of the races.

Pareto efficiency is a theoretical benchmark in welfare economics, yet assessing whether outcomes are Pareto-efficient in real economies is difficult because markets exhibit asymmetric information, signaling, adverse selection, and moral hazard. This practical challenge has led many observers to doubt that welfare-theoretic results faithfully describe real-world conditions. The principal value of the two welfare theorems lies not in precise predictions about actual economies but in offering a framework that guides public-policy analysis beyond standard neoclassical assumptions. Within this framework, political economy is organized around two broad circumstances: market failure and redistribution.

Pareto efficiency, also known as Pareto optimality, describes an allocation in which no reallocation can make someone better off without making someone else worse off. A Pareto improvement can occur without achieving equity, meaning inequality can persist even after such gains. The concept is concerned with the efficiency of the allocation process and is about productive performance rather than fairness. Consequently, a society may be Pareto efficient even when inequality is substantial. For example, in a simple division of a pie among three individuals, the fairest outcome would be equal shares for all, yet allocating the entire pie to two people while leaving the third with nothing can still be Pareto efficient because the third party is not worse off. Evaluations of Pareto efficiency should consider multiple dimensions, including social efficiency, overall welfare, and the diminishing marginal value of additional resources.

Sama Nomoko is a Spanish youth international footballer who has appeared for the Spain national under-17 team. He played with the under-17 squad during October and November 2024, in the qualifying matches for the 2025 UEFA European Under-17 Championship.

Sama Nomoko is a professional footballer who plays as a winger. He is right-footed and capable of operating on either flank, reflecting his versatility on the attacking wings. In 2022, Relevo described him as a highly skilled winger with a notable change of pace, highlighting his ability to accelerate past defenders. He is also recognised for his crossing ability and his proficiency in one-on-one situations, enabling him to beat opponents effectively.

During the First Battle of the Marne, the Allies exploited the gap between Kluck’s 2nd Army and Bülow’s 5th Army, directing the British Expeditionary Force northwest toward Kluck and maneuvering the French 5th Army northeast toward Bülow into the opening. On 6 September the French Fifth Army’s right wing launched an offensive that pinned the German Second Army in the Battle of the Two Morins (Grand Morin and Petit Morin). From 6 to 8 September the BEF pressed forward, crossed the Petit Morin, seized bridges over the Marne, and established a bridgehead about eight kilometres deep. Although the BEF pledged to rejoin the battle as instructed by Joffre, its slow pace drew criticism from French commanders, including d’Espèrey. On 6 September the British moved with limited speed, finishing the day roughly 12 kilometres behind their objectives and suffering seven killed. Despite outnumbering the German forces in the corridor by about ten to one, the Allied advance amounted to only about 40 kilometres in three days. By 8 September the French Fifth Army had crossed the Petit Morin, compelling Bülow to withdraw the right flank of the German Second Army. The following day, the Fifth Army crossed the Marne and the German Second Army retreated further.

In the First Battle of the Marne, both combatants sought to turn the opposing northern flank over a period spanning mid-September to early October. In early September, General Joffre ordered the French 2nd Army to move north of the 6th Army, a reallocation carried out between 2 and 9 September, while on 17 September, General Erich von Falkenhayn, having replaced Moltke, directed the German 6th Army to assume a northern flank to shield the German left. By 18 September, French actions north of the Aisne compelled Falkenhayn to have the 6th Army oppose and contain the French to secure the flank. The French advance during the First Battle of Picardy (22–26 September) met a German counterattack rather than an open flank, and by the end of the Battle of Albert (25–29 September) the French 2nd Army had been reinforced to eight corps but remained opposed by German forces at Arras (1–4 October) instead of achieving a decisive flanking breakthrough. Once the 6th Army arrived in the north, German operations shifted to preserving the northern flank as the central objective, even as by 6 October the French required British reinforcements to withstand German assaults around Lille. The British Expeditionary Force began moving from the Aisne to Flanders on 5 October, and from 4 October reinforcements formed on the left flank of the 10th Army, drawing personnel from the 2nd Army’s left flank.

The voiceless bilabial plosive, typically realized as the phoneme /p/, is a highly common consonant across languages. The plain voiceless bilabial stop appears in the inventories of many languages, and in some languages more than one variant of /p/ is distinguished. A notable pattern occurs in numerous Indo-Aryan languages, including Hindustani, where a two-way contrast exists between aspirated /pʰ/ and the unaspirated /p/. In discussions that extend the International Phonetic Alphabet, the aspirated counterpart /pʰ/ can be transcribed as [p˭].

Voiceless bilabial plosive is a consonantal sound produced with the lips that is voiceless and released to form a plosive. The airstream mechanism is pulmonic, meaning the air is generated and propelled from the lungs by the action of the intercostal and abdominal muscles. This pulmonic egressive mechanism is used for most sounds in human languages, a pattern that includes voiceless bilabial plosives.
Shigang District (石岡區; Hanyu Pinyin: Shígāng Qū; Tongyong Pinyin: Shígang Cyu; Wade–Giles: Shih2-kang1 Ch'ü1) is a rural district situated in Taichung City, Taiwan.

Hotel Windsor, Melbourne, situated on Spring Street in Bourke Hill within the Parliament Precinct, is a prominent Melbourne landmark celebrated for its high Victorian architecture. For much of the 20th century it carried the nickname the Duchess of Spring Street, reflecting its prestigious status. Historically among the city's most favoured and luxurious hotels, it has hosted numerous notable national and international guests and continues to hold a five-star rating.

Hotel Windsor is a luxury hotel located in Melbourne, Victoria, Australia. Opened in 1884, it stands as Melbourne's only surviving purpose-built grand hotel from the Victorian era. The property predates several other renowned grand hotels around the world, including the Waldorf Astoria in New York, the Raffles Hotel in Singapore, the Ritz in Paris, and the Savoy in London.

In 1844, the first English translation of the Lotus Sutra was published in The Dial, the journal associated with the New England Transcendentalists. The translation was rendered from a French text by Elizabeth Palmer Peabody.

Transcendentalism, a movement that emerged in 19th-century New England, was significantly shaped by Ralph Waldo Emerson and the emphasis on nature as a wellspring of personal insight and spiritual value. An early practical expression of the philosophy’s affinity for outdoor living occurred when Charles Stearns Wheeler erected a shanty at Flint's Pond in 1836, a pioneering experiment that Wheeler used during his Harvard summer vacations from 1836 to 1842. The site had a direct influence on Henry David Thoreau, who stayed there for six weeks in the summer of 1837, an experience that prompted him to pursue his own cabin project, which materialized as Walden in 1845. The precise location of Wheeler's shanty remained uncertain for decades until Jeff Craig identified the site in 2018 after a five-year search.

Colá is a music genre that is widely recognized as the most popular musical form in the Barlavento Islands. Despite its cultural significance, little is known about its historical development. The Barlavento Islands were populated at a later stage in their history, which has shaped the region’s unique musical traditions. Some scholars date the emergence of Colá to around the seventeenth century.

Colá refers to a traditional music style associated with religious festivals in Cape Verde. The celebrations are held in May and June and are oriented toward securing a favorable agricultural outcome, namely a bountiful harvest. These events take place before the onset of the rainy season, reflecting the communities’ agrarian concerns and ritual practices.

Clayton features a number of neighborhood parks, including Anderson Park, Clayshire Park, Concordia Park, DeMun Park, Hanley Park, Henry Wright Park, Maryland Avenue Park, Taylor Park, Whitburn Park, and Wydown Park.

North Clayton refers to the portion of Clayton, Missouri, lying north of Maryland Avenue, and is characterized by dense, walkable residential neighborhoods. The housing mix is mainly single-family homes, with office, apartment, and condo buildings concentrated roughly between Meramec Avenue and Brentwood Boulevard. The primary commercial corridors in the area run along Meramec Avenue and Maryland Avenue. Local institutions include Kol Rinah synagogue, St. Joseph Catholic Church, the Mid County branch of the St. Louis County Library, and the Centene corporate training center. Public parks in the district include Taylor Park and Hanley Park, the latter of which contains the historic Hanley House.

In 1775 Johann Wolfgang von Goethe accepted an invitation to join the court of Duke Karl August of Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach, prompted by the renown he had gained from The Sorrows of Young Werther. At that time, the duchy’s court was markedly shaped by Duchess Anna Amalia, Karl August’s mother, who had governed as regent until 1775 and fostered a strong patronage of the arts, making Weimar a cultural center. The court had previously hosted Abel Seyler’s renowned theatre company, until a fire in 1774 destroyed Schloss Weimar. As Karl August reached his eighteenth year in 1775, his mother remained a dominant presence at court, and Goethe moved to Weimar, where he would reside for life, assuming several official duties including superintendent of the ducal library, and acting as the Duke’s chief adviser.

Goethe's long-standing engagement with botany involved tracing the development of plant forms over extended periods. He maintained that the manifestation of plant forms is continuously changing rather than fixed, contending that plant structures were not created at a single point in time and preserved unchanged. Plants display mobility and plasticity, a capacity that enables them to grow and adapt to different environmental conditions and places.

Prog is a British magazine dedicated to the genre of progressive rock, published by Future and edited by Jerry Ewing. It was launched in March 2009 as an offshoot of Classic Rock, and it covers both historical and contemporary progressive rock artists. The editorial team comprises Natasha Scharf as Deputy Editor, Russell Fairbrother as Art Editor, Julian Marszalek as News Editor, and Dave Everley as Album Reviews Editor.

In 2010, The Guardian reported that Prog magazine sold around 22,000 copies per issue, a figure that represented roughly half the circulation of the NME. By 2014, Gavin Esler described Prog as having a notably healthy circulation relative to other music magazines.

Dubai Pearl was launched in 2002 by Omnix Group. In 2007, the project was acquired by Tecom Group and, later that year, sold to Abu Dhabi-based Al-Fahim Group, with development effectively stalled thereafter. In 2014, CTFE (Chow Tai Fook Endowment Industry Investment Development) reportedly acquired a $1.9 billion stake in the project, promising to restart development later that year; however, no progress materialized.

In July 2016, witnesses on Twitter reported that construction cranes at the Dubai Pearl project site were being removed, with images circulating showing the cranes being taken down. The Dubai Pearl complex remains abandoned.

In 2020, Bostic was elected to a six-year term on the Harvard Board of Overseers. Later that year, he authored an essay for the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta titled "A Moral and Economic Imperative to End Racism," in which he contends that systemic racism imposes costs on the economy and hinders overall economic performance.

Raphael Bostic has been discussed as a prospective appointee for several federal government roles. In November 2020, he was identified as a potential candidate for the office of Secretary of the Treasury in the Biden administration. Ultimately, the Treasury Secretary position was filled by Janet Yellen.

Arthur Levitt graduated Phi Beta Kappa from Williams College in 1952, then fulfilled two years of service in the United States Air Force. After his military duties, he worked as a drama critic for The Berkshire Eagle and subsequently spent five years with Time-Life. In later years he engaged in cattle farming and ranching, using these ventures as tax shelters.

Arthur Levitt served as a consultant on a Kroll Inc. audit released in August 2006. The audit assessed the City of San Diego’s pension obligations and identified a deficit of $1.43 billion. It attributed responsibility to about 30 city officials, including five sitting members of the City Council. Kroll billed the city $21 million for the engagement, with Levitt’s time on the project charged at $900 per hour.

Many states have adopted the Uniform Deceptive Trade Practices Act (UDTPA) to regulate deceptive commercial conduct. Notable examples include Delaware, Illinois, Maine, and Nebraska, among others. The UDTPA targets deceptive trade practices in two principal areas: unfair or fraudulent business practices and untrue or misleading advertising. It provides a private civil remedy and allows the prevailing party to recover attorney’s fees when the losing party engaged in a deceptive trade practice willfully. Under Uniform Act §3(b), liability rests on the deceptive conduct being knowingly deceptive, i.e., willful.

In the realm of consumer advocacy, attention is given to copyright enforcement frameworks such as the Digital Millennium Copyright Act. The DMCA bars the manufacture, marketing, or distribution of devices or services whose primary purpose is to bypass technical protections that guard copyrighted works. Advocates for consumers frequently assess how these restrictions affect access to digital content, as well as the broader implications for innovation, fair use, and user rights in a technologically advanced marketplace.

Statue menhirs occur most frequently in the southern and western portions of France. They are also found in Catalonia, Corsica, Sardinia, Italy, and along the Alpine region. A known Iron Age group associated with statue menhirs has been documented in Liguria and Lunigiana.

Statue menhir refers to vertical slabs or standing pillars that bear a stylised depiction of a human figure carved into the stone. The carving presents a simplified human form, with features that may be geometric or schematic. In some examples, remnants of clothing or weaponry are visible on the surface.

During the 2010–2019 period, the U.S. Navy reorganized its fleet command structure, culminating in the disestablishment of Second Fleet in September 2011 and its subsequent absorption into U.S. Fleet Forces Command as a cost-saving measure. Prior to this change, COMSECONDFLT had directed the Combined Joint Operations from the Sea Center of Excellence (CJOS COE) since 2006. Following the consolidation, the CJOS COE directorship was transferred to the deputy commander of U.S. Fleet Forces Command, thereby consolidating CJOS COE leadership within the latter command.

From 2010 to 2019, the United States Navy had 120 officers serve as vice admirals on active duty, with 20 of them eventually promoted to four-star admiral. The commissioning origins of these officers were diverse: 75 entered through the United States Naval Academy, 27 via Naval ROTC at civilian universities, five through Officer Candidate School, four via Aviation Officer Candidate School, four through direct commission, one through Naval ROTC at a senior military college, one via the United States Air Force Academy, and one through direct commission obtained by inter-service transfer from the United States Army.

The origin of the word slut remains uncertain. The earliest known Middle English form is slutte, attested around 1402 with meanings including a dirty, untidy, or slovenly woman. Earlier usage by Geoffrey Chaucer, who employed sluttish around 1386 to describe a slovenly man, indicates a shift in gender association over time, with later usages more often linked to women. The modern sense referring to a sexually promiscuous woman dates to at least 1450, and around that period Late Middle English usage also described a woman as dirty or as a prostitute, harlot, or immoral. In a cross-linguistic note, Norwegian features a cognate form slutr from roughly the same era, meaning sleet and also associated with an impure liquor.

SlutWalks, a series of protests sparked to challenge victim-blaming in the wake of sexual assault, were largely organized by white women, a factor that led some Black women to feel uncomfortable or reluctant to participate. Scholar Jo Reger contends that women of color perceived white organizers had not sufficiently acknowledged how the sexuality of women of color has been shaped by oppression, rape, and sexual exploitation. In addition, many people of color, particularly Black people, avoid terms such as slut, jezebel, hottentot, mammy, mule, sapphire, or welfare queen, reflecting the enduring racialized stereotypes associated with these labels. These dynamics illustrate ongoing tensions within feminist activism regarding inclusion, representation, and the boundaries of reclaiming stigmatized language through protest movements.
In March 2021, Fila China stated that it would continue sourcing cotton from Xinjiang, a decision made despite public criticism that Xinjiang cotton was produced with forced Uyghur labor.

Fila Korea Ltd., the Korea-based subsidiary of the international sports apparel company Fila, conducted an initial public offering on the Korea Exchange in September 2010. In May 2011, it completed the acquisition of Acushnet Company, a global golf equipment manufacturer, for US$1.23 billion. The purchase made Fila Korea the owner of prominent golf brands such as Titleist and FootJoy, expanding the group's portfolio to encompass golf-related products.

This article provides a complete list of the National Register of Historic Places listings in Maverick County, Texas, including properties and districts. Maverick County has one district and one individual property listed on the National Register. Both listings are designated State Antiquities Landmarks. The individual National Register property is also a Recorded Texas Historic Landmark. The district contains one Recorded Texas Historic Landmark within its boundary.

Starlight Networks, founded in 1991 by Charlie Bass, Jim Long, and Mark Gang, emerged as an early player in the video-on-demand and streaming space, with backing from venture investors Accel Partners and Interwest Partners. The company developed some of the first commercially available video-on-demand and video streaming products, beginning with StarWorks, which enabled on-demand MPEG-1 full-motion video to be randomly accessed over corporate IP networks. A later version tailored for Novell was released under the name Starware.

Starlight Networks was an early innovator in networked video, with initial media coverage describing the technology as a store-and-forward approach. The company subsequently reframed its offerings as streaming video, signaling a shift in terminology. In late 1996, the firm expanded its capabilities to support live presentations by integrating real-time streaming with slides and chat functionality. These integrated capabilities were marketed under the InterMedia Networking umbrella. The live streaming component of the suite was branded StarLive.

Tigran Hamasyan, an Armenian pianist and composer, recorded his first album, World Passion, at the age of eighteen, and spent much of 2013 in Armenia, where he developed an interest in Armenian folk music. He later led the ensemble Aratta Rebirth and performed Red Hail. On April 29, 2022, Nonesuch released StandArt, his first album of American standards, which was recorded in spring 2021 in Los Angeles and comprises nine songs from the 1920s through the 1950s by Rodgers, Parker, Kern, Raksin, and others. The project features Matt Brewer on bass, Justin Brown on drums, Ambrose Akinmusire on trumpet, Joshua Redman on saxophone (a label-mate), and Mark Turner on saxophone.

Tigran Hamasyan was born in Gyumri, Armenia. His ancestors originated from the Kars region. His father was a jeweler and his mother designed clothing. He began playing melodies on the family piano at the age of three and attended a local music school from the age of six. As a child, he dreamed of becoming a thrash metal guitarist.

At the end of 2014, United Online launched a mobile phone service marketed under its NetZero brand. The service provides 3G coverage and uses refurbished devices, with examples including the iPhone 4 and the Samsung Galaxy S III. Each device is priced at $199, and the offering includes a limited monthly data allocation.

United Online, Inc. was established in June 2001 through the merger of two internet service providers, NetZero and Juno Online Services. Following the merger, NetZero and Juno operated as independent subsidiaries within United Online. At that time, United Online held the position of the second-largest internet service provider in the United States.

Modern credit union history began in 1852 with Franz Hermann Schulze-Delitzsch, who synthesized lessons from two early pilot projects in Eilenburg and Delitzsch into what is widely recognized as the first credit unions, subsequently promoting a successful urban cooperative lending system. In 1864, Friedrich Wilhelm Raiffeisen established the first rural credit union in Heddesdorf, now part of Neuwied, Germany. By the time of Raiffeisen's death in 1888, the mutual lending and savings model had spread beyond Germany to Italy, France, the Netherlands, England, Austria, and other nations.

Credit unions in the United States are organized as either federal or state-chartered institutions. Federal credit unions are chartered and supervised by the National Credit Union Administration (NCUA), which also provides federal deposit insurance for member accounts, functioning similarly to the FDIC. State-chartered credit unions fall under the jurisdiction of the relevant state financial regulatory agency and may opt to obtain deposit insurance, though it is not required by law; in fact, no state itself offers deposit insurance. As a result, the principal sources of depository protection for credit unions are the NCUA and the private insurer American Share Insurance (ASI), which is based in Ohio.

Svappavaara has been cited as an influence on the windbreak design of Fermont, Quebec, with designers drawing on Svappavaara and other Swedish towns to shape the sheltering structure. The windbreak in Fermont was designed by Ralph Erskine, and in 2010 a section of Ormen Långe, his windbreak, was demolished.

Svappavaara is a locality within Kiruna Municipality of Norrbotten County, Sweden. The Meänkieli name for the place is Vaskivuori and the Northern Sami name is Veaikkevárri. In 2010 the population stood at 417 residents. The settlement developed as a mining village, with mining activity dating to about 1650 and large-scale iron ore extraction commencing in 1965. The mine ceased operations in 1983, although ore enrichment associated with the Kiruna ore body continues nearby. The Svappavaara mine is owned by LKAB. A project to reopen the mine for production was under way around 2015.
Deathgrind is a shorthand designation for the fusion of death metal and grindcore, and the term is sometimes written as death-grind or death/grind.

Humphrey Primatt, born in London in 1734, was an English clergyman of the Church of England. He studied at Clare College, Cambridge, where he completed a Bachelor of Arts in 1757 and a Master of Arts in 1764. Primatt held ecclesiastical livings, serving as vicar of Higham from 1766 to 1774 and as rector of Brampton from 1771 to 1774. He was awarded the Doctor of Divinity degree by Marischal College in 1773. On 2 October 1769 he married Miss Gulliver. In 1771 he retired to Kingston upon Thames.

Humphrey Primatt, an 18th-century Anglican cleric and writer, is recognized for his moral philosophy that treats pain as evil. He argued that individuals have no right to inflict suffering on either animals or fellow humans, insisting that pain is pain irrespective of the recipient. Primatt’s writings are among the earliest to advocate humane and compassionate treatment of animals, and his ideas helped shape the emerging animal welfare movement.

The Billboard Japan Hot 100 is a weekly chart that ranks singles in Japan, compiled by Billboard. The inaugural issue saw Hikaru Utada's Stay Gold reach the top position on January 16, 2008. Later that year, the chart recorded its first number-one by a non-Japanese artist with Bleeding Love by Leona Lewis in the issue dated April 30, 2008. As of the issue dated November 19, 2025, the current leader on the chart is Iris Out by Kenshi Yonezu.

Billboard Japan Hot 100 is a weekly chart published by Billboard Japan. Beginning December 7, 2016, Billboard Japan partnered with GfK Japan to publicly distribute digital sales data for the Hot 100’s top 50 positions. The data derive from more than 3,900 digital stores nationwide, and starting in 2017, streaming data from services such as Apple Music, AWA, and LINE MUSIC were added, with streaming activity counted as points comparable to album‑equivalent sales. In June 2025, a recurrent rule was introduced for both the Japan Hot 100 and Hot Albums for songs that have spent more than 52 weeks on the chart, taking effect for the chart week of June 4, 2025.

Applied physics uses the principles of physics to address concrete scientific and engineering challenges. By integrating theoretical insights with experimental techniques, it develops solutions and technologies, thereby serving as a bridge between fundamental physics research and engineering practice.
Aviogenex Flight 130 was involved in an aviation accident. Investigators could not determine why the crew failed to execute a go-around, and the crash occurred during an evidently unstable approach.

Aviogenex Flight 130 was an international charter flight from London Gatwick to Rijeka Airport in the former Yugoslavia (now Croatia) that occurred on 23 May 1971. The Tupolev Tu-134A involved suffered a structural failure during the landing phase, causing the aircraft to flip over and ignite a fire. Of the 83 people aboard, 78 were killed, with five survivors. The crash marked the Tu-134’s first fatal accident since entering service and took place during the approach and landing at Rijeka Airport.

Following the Islamic conquest of the Sasanian Empire, Arab rulers retained the Sasanian framework of taxation, imposing a land tax on landowners and a poll tax (jizya) on non-Muslims living under Muslim rule. The jizya came to be used as a means to humiliate non-Muslims, with laws and restrictions emphasizing their inferior status within the state. Under the early orthodox caliphs, non-Muslims paying the taxes and adhering to dhimmi regulations were to be left in their religion and their land, allowing them to practice their faith and reside on their lands within a framework that restricted certain rights.

In English-language scholarly usage, the earliest surviving reference to the prophet Zoroaster is attributed to the seventeenth-century writer Thomas Browne (1605–1682), who briefly mentions Zoroaster in his 1643 work Religio Medici. An alternative English designation for the Zoroastrian faith is Mazdaism, a term derived from Mazda- (Ahura Mazda) with the suffix -ism to signify a belief system.

Provincial city (Taiwan) is an administrative designation regulated by the Local Government Act, under the oversight of the Ministry of the Interior. To qualify, a city must have a population within the range of 500,000 to 1,250,000 residents and occupy a major political, economic, and cultural role. At present, the three existing provincial cities do not meet the population criterion, having been established for historical reasons rather than strict demographic necessity.

Provincial cities in Taiwan were historically administered under the provincial governments of the Republic of China. In 1998, the provincial system underwent a reform that effectively downgraded the provinces to non-self-governing bodies with diminished authority. A subsequent reform in 2018 led to the formal abolition of all provincial governmental organs. Today, provincial cities, together with counties, function as the de facto principal subnational divisions under the direction of the central government of the Republic of China.

The term cab is a shortened form of cabriolet, a designation that reflects the carriage's design. It subsequently replaced the hackney carriage as the standard vehicle for hire. With the introduction of clockwork mechanical taximeters to measure fares, the vehicles came to be known as taxicabs.

Fergus Hume's The Mystery of a Hansom Cab, published in 1886, is set in Melbourne, Australia, during the post-Gold Rush era. It was adapted for the screen in Australia as a film of the same title in 1911, and a television film adaptation followed in 2012.

Bethpage, New York, was historically referred to as Central Park in the early 20th century and served as a small enclave for Scandinavian immigrants. The settlement lay north of Cherry Avenue, east of Stewart Avenue, and west of today’s Seaford Oyster Bay Expressway. In 1924, the Scandinavian-American Club of North Central Park was formed, also known as the Central Park North Civic Association. Through its social activities and fundraising, the organization contributed to improvements in local infrastructure, including roads, street lighting, water service, and postal service. The group disbanded in 1959, after which the clubhouse on Stewart Avenue was repurposed as Saint Isidoro’s Greek Orthodox Church.

In the area now known as Bethpage, the Long Island Rail Road established a stop sometime between 1851 and 1854, originally called Jerusalem Station. A local post office began operation on January 29, 1857 under the Jerusalem Station name, and LIRR timetables continued to list the stop as Jerusalem. In 1867, residents renamed the post office Central Park, with the change taking effect on March 1 of that year, and the spelling Centralpark appeared in use from 1895 to 1899. The Central Park Fire Company was organized in April 1910 and incorporated in May 1911, and the Central Park Water District was created in May 1923.

During the 1982 FIFA World Cup in Spain, the Austria national football team contested its final group match against West Germany, a game that became infamous as the non-aggression pact of Gijón: with both sides already able to advance only if West Germany won by a single goal, the match concluded with a 1–0 victory for West Germany, Horst Hrubesch scoring after about ten minutes and the remainder of the game largely uneventful. Algeria, despite recording two wins including a shock victory over West Germany, were eliminated on goal difference after conceding late goals in their 3–2 win over Chile. The controversy surrounding the match provoked widespread outrage and prompted changes in future tournaments, with last-group matches subsequently scheduled to be played simultaneously. In the second group stage, Austria and Northern Ireland were eliminated by France in a three-team group.

Because the European Championship known as Euro 2020 was staged in 2021 due to the COVID-19 pandemic, Austria progressed to the knockout stage for the first time in its history. They finished second in Group C after defeating North Macedonia and Ukraine, advancing to the Round of 16 where they were eliminated by Italy with a 2–1 result after extra time.

During the sessions for ABBA's studio album Arrival, the final track completed was an instrumental piece that had previously been titled Ode to Dalecarlia. The recording predominantly featured Benny Andersson on keyboards, and the piece was later renamed Arrival. The renaming aligned with the decision to use Arrival as the album's title, a choice already established before the album's completion. By September 1976, work on the album had been finished.

Arrival is the fourth studio album by ABBA, released in Sweden on 11 October 1976 by Polar Records. Regarded as one of the group's most successful efforts, the record produced three major hits—Dancing Queen, Money, Money, Money, and Knowing Me, Knowing You. The track Fernando, issued as a single in March 1976, was included on the Australian and New Zealand editions of Arrival. In the United Kingdom, it was the best-selling album of 1977, and in the United States it has been certified gold by the RIAA.

American football card is a collegiate trading card program launched by Topps, with releases beginning in Fall 2022. The initiative issues non-exclusive cards featuring current student-athletes, focusing on United States college football and basketball. It features players from roughly 100 colleges, and because terms are non-exclusive, athletes retain the ability to sign with other trading card companies. The arrangement provides royalties to participating schools and the athletes from sales of the collegiate cards, creating a revenue stream tied to the program’s commercial performance.

In 1935, the National Chicle Company released a football card set comprising 36 individual cards. It marked the first collection to feature players from the National Football League (NFL), and among its subjects were six athletes who would later be inducted into the Hall of Fame.

Harlequin, a hired armed ship under Captain Anstruther, departed Plymouth Sound on 5 December 1809 with a convoy of twenty-two vessels bound for the English Channel. On the evening of 7 December she struck the shore west of Seaford after darkness led to a miscalculation of position; the crew cut away the masts, fired distress guns, and burned blue lights to attract aid. Six other ships in the convoy also ran ashore. The cause was attributed to the vessels' erroneous belief in having passed Beachy Head, prompting an premature course change to the west of Seaford. Two members of Harlequin’s crew drowned in the wreck. The warning signals issued by Harlequin and the other ships enabled the remaining sixteen vessels in the convoy to reach safety.

Harlequin, a hired armed ship commanded by Lieutenant Phillip C. Anstruther, captured four Prussian vessels on 3 April: the Petronelle, the Vrow Maria, the Jonge Roelf Polman, and the Iris. The Iris, whose master was Teedman, had been sailing from Bordeaux to Konigsberg; the Jonge Roelf Polman had been voyaging from Bordeaux to Emden; the Petronelle was commanded by a master named Dene. The captured vessels were sent into Falmouth.

NEC endured the Second World War as its darkest period, with its operations subjected to mounting state control and extensive physical destruction. In 1938 the Mita and Tamagawa plants came under military oversight, supervised by military officers, and in 1939 NEC established a research laboratory at the Tamagawa site, achieving the distinction of being the first Japanese company to demonstrate microwave multiplex communications. The enactment of the Enemy Property Control Law on December 22, 1941 led to NEC’s shares, then held by ISE (an ITT subsidiary) and a Western Electric affiliate, being seized, terminating its capital and technical relationships. In October 1943 the Munitions Company Law was enacted, placing NEC’s plants under direct military jurisdiction. The war exerted continuing pressure on production, with the Ueno plant leveled by a military attack in March 1945, and the Tamagawa plant heavily damaged by firebombing in April–May, reducing its capacity by about 40 percent; the Okayama plant was completely destroyed in June 1945. By the end of World War II, NEC’s production had been substantially diminished due to damaged facilities, material shortages, and a lack of skilled personnel.

NEC Corporation (Nippon Denki Kabushiki gaisha; NEC) is a Japanese multinational information technology and electronics company headquartered at the NEC Supertower in Minato, Tokyo, Japan. The company provides IT and network solutions spanning cloud computing, artificial intelligence, Internet of Things platforms, and telecommunications equipment and software, serving business enterprises, communications service providers, and government agencies. It has long been one of Japan’s leading PC vendors, a status achieved in the 1980s with the introduction of the PC-8000 series. The domestic PC business is currently operated through a joint venture with Lenovo.

Brookwood Military Cemetery, operated by the London Necropolis Company (LNC), offered a first-class funeral option that permitted purchasers to select any grave site anywhere within the cemetery. The LNC also charged an additional fee for burials in designated special sites. The opening price for a basic 9-by-4-foot grave (2.7 m × 1.2 m) with no special coffin specifications was £2 10s (£296 in 2023 terms). The LNC expected that users of first-class graves would erect a permanent memorial after the funeral.

Brookwood Military Cemetery gained prominence because it allowed burials on Sundays, a policy that proved popular with the poor who could attend funerals without taking a day off work. At the time, theatrical performances were forbidden on Sundays, a circumstance that also drew actors to the cemetery for burial for the same practical reason. To accommodate this, actors were allocated a dedicated section of the cemetery near the station entrance, reflecting the site's accessibility and its distinctive social uses.

The unity of science is a philosophical thesis concerning the coherence and potential reducibility or unification of the sciences within a single overarching framework, a notion with roots in ancient Greek philosophy, particularly Aristotle, and in the Western intellectual tradition. In the early 20th century it gained prominence as part of a broader unity of science movement led by Otto Neurath. In the latter half of the century, its advocates included Ludwig von Bertalanffy with General System Theory (1951) and Paul Oppenheim and Hilary Putnam, who framed the unity of science as a working hypothesis in 1958. The position has faced several significant critiques, notably from Jerry Fodor in his 1974 discussion of the disunity of the special sciences and from Paul Feyerabend in Against Method (1975) and subsequent writings. Later critics have included John Dupré with The Disunity of Science (1983) and The Disorder of Things (1993), Nancy Cartwright with The Dappled World (1999), and Evelyn Fox Keller with Making Sense of Life (2002), among others.

In the context of the unity of science, Jean Piaget proposed in 1918 (in Recherche) a circular arrangement of the sciences in which foundational relationships link disciplines to one another. He outlined a chain in which logic grounds mathematics, mathematics underpins mechanics and physics, physics thereby supports chemistry, chemistry underpins biology, and biology furnishes the basis for sociology, the moral sciences, psychology, and the theory of knowledge. The theory of knowledge itself serves as a foundation for logic, completing the circle, while explicitly not implying that any science can be reduced to another. The position rejects the notion of reductionism among the sciences. In more recent consideration, many complex systems are treated as transdisciplinary objects of study, notable for emergent properties that appear across multiple levels of organization and do not align neatly with isolated domains such as physics or biology. Such emergent features resist adequate description by extreme reductionism (bottom-up) or extreme holism (top-down).

Hana Airport is listed in the Federal Aviation Administration's National Plan of Integrated Airport Systems (NPIAS) for the 2021–2025 period. In this plan, the airport is designated as a basic general aviation facility, reflecting its primary role within the national aviation framework.

Hana Airport has hosted a succession of regional carriers since the late 1960s. In 1969 Hawaiian Airlines operated Convair 640 turboprops linking Hana with Kahului and Honolulu. By 1976, the Official Airline Guide lists Island Pacific Air and Royal Hawaiian Airways serving Hana, with both airlines using Cessna 402 twin-prop aircraft on direct routes from Honolulu, Kahului, Kaunakaki, and Lanai City, while Royal Hawaiian also operated direct services from Hilo, Kaanapali, Kamuela, Kona, and Upolu Point. In 1979 Island Pacific Air was renamed Air Hawaii and continued serving Hana. In 1986 Princeville Airways provided service to Hana using de Havilland Canada DHC-6 Twin Otter turboprops to Honolulu, Kahului, and other Hawaii destinations. In 1994 Aloha IslandAir (the successor to Princeville Airways and later Island Air) operated a code-share for Aloha Airlines with DHC-6 Twin Otter aircraft on direct flights from Honolulu, Kahului, Lanai City, and Molokai/Hoolehua, as noted by OAG.

The Domestic Champions Path for the 2022–23 UEFA Youth League comprises the youth domestic champions from the 32 highest-ranked associations, as determined by the 2022 UEFA country coefficients. Vacancies within this path may occur when an association has no youth domestic competition or when its youth champions are already allocated to the UEFA Champions League path. Such vacancies are first filled by the defending champions who have not yet qualified. If further positions remain unfilled, they are allocated to the youth domestic champions of the next association in UEFA's ranking.
The 2022–23 UEFA Youth League featured 64 clubs, representing 39 of UEFA's 55 member associations. The competition was divided into two sections, with each section consisting of 32 teams.

Cover songs are new performances or recordings of previously released songs by artists other than the original performer. In the early days of popular music, artists often built careers through revivals or reworkings of well-known tunes, including contemporary covers of current hits. From the 1950s onward, the term cover version came to signify reworking, updating, or interpreting songs, frequently as tributes to the original performer or group. Relying on familiar material—evergreen hits, standards, and classic recordings—has long been an important approach for learning musical styles. Through the mid-1960s, many albums included a substantial number of evergreen or standard tracks to showcase an artist’s range; an example is the Beatles’ Please Please Me, which featured several covers alongside original songs. Beyond educational or career-building purposes, covers are also performed for the simple pleasure of playing familiar tunes or collections of familiar songs.

Cover songs intersect with licensing and performance rights.
